## John Boyd · The OODA loop
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/boyd/ooda/
Source: Boyd's briefing, Patterns of Conflict
Tags: Deep read, John Boyd, Fast means turning, not moving

He was a fighter instructor who could win from any position in forty seconds. What 'fast' meant in the loop he built.

### Q: What actually happened?
Boyd compressed all conflict into one loop: observe, orient, decide, act. The claim isn't that each step should be quick, but that you should operate inside the opponent's loop: you finish two cycles while he finishes one, so what he observes is the world your last move made — every reaction fights a version of you that no longer exists. Facing an ambiguous, fast-changing environment, his loop slows until he collapses from the inside. In Korea the outmatched F-86 posted a lopsided kill ratio; Boyd's explanation was hydraulic controls — it switched between manoeuvres faster.

### The parts · The bottleneck is almost always orient
Observe, decide and act can all be sped up with tools. The slow one is orient: fitting new information into your existing frame. The more successful the old frame, the less new information gets in — organisations do see the change, they just file it under the old map.
e.g. The data showed the new channel growing on Monday and it wasn't called a trend until the quarterly review. Those six weeks were orient, not observation.

### The parts · Getting inside means producing rapid change
You don't wait to get faster; you make him slower. Keep the rhythm and direction of your moves unpredictable so his last read expires before he can act on it. He spends more time understanding you and less executing his own plan. That is how initiative changes hands.
e.g. A predictable opponent is the easiest kind: his launches and promotions are on a calendar. Come off the calendar and every response he makes is late.

### The parts · Turning fast requires low internal friction
Boyd's prescription for organisations wasn't acceleration, it was less friction: shared intent, mutual trust, authority pushed down. Every approval layer is delay in the loop; every ounce of suspicion is paid for in confirmations. Trust isn't a soft metric. It is the loop speed.
e.g. Two equally able teams: one acts and reports, one asks first. The gap isn't the people, it's the delegation.

### Q: How do I use it today?
Where you are: you and your competitor are both accelerating, and you're buying tools for every step.
Ask first: which step is our loop stuck on? Usually the one where we saw it and didn't change the frame.
Where it goes wrong: turning fast into thrashing, motion with no direction; or internally, adding speed without removing friction, which just makes the mess arrive sooner.

### Lines to keep
Observe, orient, decide, act.
Operate inside his loop, and give him an ambiguous, fast-changing world.
Machines don't fight and terrain doesn't fight. People do.

========================================================================
## John Boyd · To be somebody, or to do something
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/boyd/to-be-or-to-do/
Source: The 'fork in the road' talk, recorded in Coram's biography
Tags: Deep read, John Boyd, The fork in the road

He made colonel and never rose again. The speech he gave every young officer who wanted to follow him.

### Q: What actually happened?
Boyd made enemies across the Pentagon: the lightweight fighter he pushed cut into too many budgets. Whenever a young officer wanted to join him he gave the same talk. You will come to a fork. One road: go along, accommodate the system, get promoted, collect the medals, and be somebody. The other: do what should be done, and get things done. Take the second and you won't rise fast, but you won't have to betray yourself. He stopped at colonel. The F-16 and American manoeuvre-warfare doctrine are full of his work.

### The parts · The two roads pay in different currencies
To be pays in position — title, grade, circle — issued by the system and revocable by it. To do pays in results: what you finished stays in the world and nobody can confiscate it. The fork is really asking which currency you intend to accumulate.
e.g. One decade: one person banked three promotions, the other three systems still running. Layoff day shows the difference in liquidity.

### The parts · Accept the price of the second road up front
Boyd didn't dress it up: no promotion, being frozen out, the cold bench — he said all of it. The honesty is in putting the bill first. People who take 'to do' and then complain about missing 'to be' rewards want both and end up with neither.
e.g. Most of the pain comes from scoring yourself on the other road's scoreboard.

### The parts · The system takes the work and withholds the credit
His designs were adopted, his theory written into doctrine, and the credit and the stars went elsewhere. That's the standard ending on this road: the results are absorbed, the person isn't crowned. Knowing that in advance moves your satisfaction to 'the thing is in use' — the only stable pay here.
e.g. Your proposal lands, packaged as your boss's win. The disgust is real. So is the proposal, running.

### Q: How do I use it today?
Where you are: a chance to move up conflicts with something that should get done.
Ask first: which currency am I accumulating? Having taken this road, am I willing to use this road's scoreboard?
Where it goes wrong: using 'to do' as consolation while nothing actually gets done; or despising 'to be' entirely, forgetting that some things can only be done from a position.

### Lines to keep
One road: promotion and medals. The other: doing what should be done.
You won't rise fast, but you won't have to betray yourself.
People, ideas, hardware — in that order.

========================================================================
## Warren Buffett · The circle of competence
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/buffett/circle-of-competence/
Source: Berkshire letters, 1996
Tags: Deep read, Warren Buffett, The edge matters more than the size

Everyone hears it as a licence to stay small. The working part is the sentence after it, and it is about the edge.

### Q: What actually happened?
The formulation in the 1996 letter is that investors need only be able to evaluate selected businesses, and — the part that gets dropped — that the size of the circle is not very important; knowing its boundaries is vital. He stayed out of technology for most of forty years and said so in public, repeatedly, while it was making other people rich. That is not an admission of limitation. It is the discipline itself, performed where everyone could see it.

### The parts · The boundary is a claim you can check
Inside the circle you can say how the thing makes money in a sentence, and say what would have to happen for it to stop. If either sentence comes out vague, you are outside, whatever your job title says.
e.g. He had used the product for years and still could not say who paid, or for what. That is outside, regardless of how familiar it felt.

### The parts · Familiarity is not competence
The most common way the boundary moves without anyone deciding is that something becomes familiar — in the news, in conversation, in the portfolio of someone you respect — and familiarity gets read as understanding.
e.g. Everyone at the table owned it, so it stopped feeling like a decision and started feeling like a default.

### The parts · Staying out has to be sayable out loud
A boundary you hold privately erodes, because there is no cost to crossing it quietly. Said in public it becomes something you would have to explain reversing, and that friction is the point.
e.g. Writing 'we don't do this, and here is why' in the team doc is what stopped it being reopened every quarter by whoever had just read an article.

### Q: How do I use it today?
Where you are: about to commit money, time or reputation to something you sort of understand.
Ask first: can you say in one sentence how it makes money, and one sentence for what would stop it? If not, you are outside the edge.
Where it goes wrong: using it as a reason never to learn anything new — the circle is meant to grow, deliberately and slowly, not to be defended forever.

### Lines to keep
The size of the circle is not very important. Knowing its boundaries is vital.
Familiarity gets read as understanding, and nobody notices the swap.
A boundary you never say out loud is one you will cross quietly.

========================================================================
## Warren Buffett · You find out at low tide
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/buffett/swimming-naked/
Source: Berkshire letters, 1992 and 2001
Tags: Deep read, Warren Buffett, Risk shows up late, on purpose

In a rising market every stroke looks good. The question is how to see the risk while it is still invisible.

### Q: What actually happened?
He used the picture repeatedly: only when the tide goes out do you discover who has been swimming naked. It points at a structural feature of risk. Leverage, mismatch and luck do not just stay hidden during a boom — they amplify returns, so the naked swimmer is the fastest one in the water. Which is why his own disciplines are all counter-cyclical, and why Berkshire has carried an amount of cash that looks like underperformance for years at a time.

### The parts · Boom-time returns have risk premium mixed in
Whoever is beating the market may be doing it with skill, or by carrying more leverage and buying less insurance. On the statement the two are indistinguishable. So read a result by asking what is left of it once the borrowing and the exposure are taken out.
e.g. The fund's three great years were one leverage decision made in the first of them, and nobody separated the two.

### The parts · Put the trunks on while the tide is in
Looking for protection at low tide means paying peak prices for the things that are scarcest in a crisis — cash, insurance, credit — if you can get them at all. Every protection has to be bought while it is not needed, which is exactly what makes it hard.
e.g. The credit line arranged in the good quarter cost almost nothing and was the reason the bad one was survivable.

### The parts · Put the tide going out into the model
You cannot know when it turns, but every decision can be run through the test: funding stops, the largest customer leaves, rates double — does this still stand? What does not stand is fragile however much it is currently earning.
e.g. Half of revenue came through one channel, and the plan for that channel closing was a sentence nobody had written.

### Q: How do I use it today?
Where you are: things are going well and the returns look like skill.
Ask first: run it through one low tide — funding stops, the big customer leaves, rates double. What is left standing?
Where it goes wrong: reading it as a reason to hold cash forever — the point is buying protection early, not declining to swim.

### Lines to keep
Only when the tide goes out do you discover who has been swimming naked.
Every protection has to be bought while it is not needed.
What cannot survive the test is fragile, however much it is earning now.

========================================================================
## John Cacioppo · Loneliness is a kind of hunger
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/cacioppo/loneliness-is-a-signal/
Source: Cacioppo & Patrick, Loneliness, 2008
Tags: Deep read, John Cacioppo, A signal, not a personality

What loneliness actually is. Why thirty years of research put it in the same category as hunger and thirst.

### Q: What actually happened?
Cacioppo spent thirty years on loneliness, and the first thing he did was tighten the definition: loneliness is not being alone. It's the gap between the connection you want and the connection you have. Which is why a crowded table can be lonely and living alone need not be. Tighten the definition and the category changes too — he filed it with hunger, thirst and pain. All of them are the body flagging something you need to survive.

### The parts · Call it a defect and you hide it, which closes the only exit
Read loneliness as a flaw in your character and the first instinct is to say nothing — which seals the one way out. As a signal it carries no shame: it doesn't say something is wrong with you, it says something needs doing.
e.g. 'I'm just not a people person.' The moment that sentence is out, every available move is switched off.

### The parts · Alone and lonely are different, so most advice aims wrong
With the definition tightened, a lot of standard advice stops working. Move to a bigger city, go to more things — all of it is the opposite of solitude, and none of it closes the gap. The test is subjective: does anyone here know you.
e.g. Dinner plans every night and emptier each time — the thing being added isn't on the ledger.

### The parts · It has physical consequences, not just unpleasant ones
Chronically lonely people show higher blood pressure, worse inflammatory markers, lighter sleep and faster cognitive decline. Cacioppo pressed this point to move the subject out of the 'being precious' box. The body is settling the bill.
e.g. Across multiple studies the effect of long-term loneliness on mortality lands in the same range as long-term smoking.

### Q: How do I use it today?
Where you are: you feel lonely, and feel embarrassed to say so.
Ask first: am I missing people being present, or people knowing me? The two answers lead to completely different moves — the first is helped by crowds, the second is not.
Where it goes wrong: hearing it as an order to widen your circle immediately, which only adds volume; or turning it back on yourself for not being outgoing enough. The signal doesn't check your personality first — extroverts get it too.

### Lines to keep
Hungry, you go find food. This is the same kind of reminder.
People near you, and people who know you, are not the same count.
It doesn't say something is wrong with you. It says something needs doing.

========================================================================
## John Cacioppo · Loneliness makes you misread faces
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/cacioppo/hypervigilance/
Source: Cacioppo's experimental work on social-threat vigilance
Tags: Deep read, John Cacioppo, The more watchful, the more alone

Why loneliness feeds itself. The loop Cacioppo found, and where you can cut it.

### Q: What actually happened?
Cacioppo's least intuitive finding: lonely people are unusually alert to social threat. Shown neutral faces in the lab, the lonelier the subject, the more likely they were to read unfriendliness into them; they also reacted faster to negative social words. His explanation was evolutionary — an individual cut off from the group has to be watchful to survive. Today that same self-protection turns on you: you read coolness as hostility, so you pull back; the other person feels the distance, and pulls back too.

### The parts · The problem isn't their attitude, it's the reading
'Things have been busy' lands as a fact for one person and as a brush-off for another. Same words in, different conclusion out, and from there completely different moves. The layer doing the work is in the middle.
e.g. No instant reply, so he doesn't want to talk to you. Most of the time he's in a meeting.

### The parts · The loop runs without anyone's help
Watchfulness makes you withdraw; withdrawing thins the relationship; the thin relationship confirms that you're not wanted. Nobody has to have rejected you for any of this to keep turning — which is why more contact alone doesn't break it.
e.g. The more you fear a no, the less you ask; the less you ask, the fewer invitations; the harder the conclusion gets.

### The parts · You break it by testing, not by pep talk
What works isn't telling yourself people do like you. It's treating the reading as a guess that could be wrong and going to check. The vigilance only loosens after the guess has been proved wrong a few times.
e.g. You're sure she's avoiding you. Ask her to something. Most of the time the answer isn't the one you rehearsed.

### Q: How do I use it today?
Where you are: you feel people around you don't much want you there, but can't point to anything specific.
Ask first: did I observe this or infer it? Write it as a sentence that could be proved wrong, then find one chance to test it.
Where it goes wrong: using this to dismiss every real slight. Some people genuinely aren't friendly. This is about a bias in reading, not a reason to doubt everything you feel.

### Lines to keep
Loneliness will read an ordinary face as unfriendly.
Nobody has to have rejected you for this to keep running.
Whether people like you is something you can test, not guess.

========================================================================
## John Cacioppo · More socialising doesn't fix it
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/cacioppo/not-more-socializing/
Source: Masi, Chen, Hawkley & Cacioppo, meta-analysis of loneliness interventions, 2011
Tags: Deep read, John Cacioppo, The meta-analysis ranks it third

The most common advice for loneliness performs worst. What came first in the data.

### Q: What actually happened?
In 2011 Cacioppo and colleagues pooled the loneliness interventions into four kinds: more chances to socialise, more social support, better social skills, and correcting how social situations get read. The first three are everyone's instinct, and none of them did much. The fourth came first — going after automatic conclusions like 'they must find me boring' and 'if I reach out I'll be a nuisance.' The reason is the same as the last piece: the stuck layer is the reading.

### The parts · When opportunity isn't scarce, adding opportunity does nothing
A university campus, a big city, a company offsite — the objective chances to socialise are plentiful, and lonely people are lonely in all of them. When the bottleneck isn't opportunity, more of it just delivers 'none of these people are mine' more often.
e.g. Ten events and you still went home alone. That usually isn't a shortage of events.

### The parts · Skills rank third, because most people aren't short of them
Filing loneliness under 'bad at talking to people' is the other wrong turn. Skills training came third in the data, because most lonely people are fine everywhere else — they can do it, they just answer on the other person's behalf at the critical moment.
e.g. Easy company all day at work, and the message saying 'lunch this weekend?' never gets sent.

### The parts · What changes is the sentence that appears on its own
The move is small: catch the automatic conclusion, write it down, ask what it rests on. 'He didn't reply' is a fact. 'He doesn't want to talk to me' is a conclusion. You added the step in between. Separate them, then look for another reading.
e.g. Rewrite 'I'm annoying him' as 'he might be busy', and send one more message tomorrow.

### Q: How do I use it today?
Where you are: you did what everyone said, went to the things, met people, and you're still lonely.
Ask first: the last time I didn't ask someone, was it for lack of a chance, or because I answered for them first? If it's the second, adding events is a road to nowhere.
Where it goes wrong: dropping social occasions altogether — opportunity isn't the most effective factor but it is still necessary; and this is not 'it's all in your head.' Some relationships genuinely aren't worth keeping.

### Lines to keep
For loneliness, changing the reading beats changing the opportunity.
Most lonely people can talk. They answer for the other person first.
The step between the fact and the conclusion is one you added.

========================================================================
## Winston Churchill · The wilderness years
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/churchill/wilderness-years/
Source: Churchill out of office, 1929–1939
Tags: Deep read, Winston Churchill, The decade nobody called him

Shut out, nobody consulting you, and no end in sight. What Churchill did with each of those days.

### Q: What actually happened?
In 1929 he went out with the government, lost the Exchequer, and held no office for the next ten years. He was not idle. He wrote for a living — the four-volume life of Marlborough and the History of the English-Speaking Peoples both came out of that decade, and the fees kept the household. At Chartwell he laid brick himself, building walls and a cottage, and had joined a bricklayers' union. When there was time left he painted. Ten years without a title, and something left his hands every day.

### The parts · When nobody calls you, make things that leave your hands
The hard part of being shut out isn't the idleness, it's not knowing whether you still count. His method was to make every day deliver: a chapter, a stretch of wall, a painting. Someone with output doesn't need an invitation to confirm they're still here.
e.g. For this stretch, fix on one thing you can finish daily, however small the finished thing is.

### The parts · The bricklaying wasn't a hobby. It put him back in his body
He built real walls, not photographs of walls. Writing spends the head; laying brick spends the arms. Use both in a day and you don't spend all of it arguing in your head with people who aren't there — which is the trap of being sidelined. Sweat pulls you out.
e.g. Put one physically hard task in the day and let it compete with the trial running in your head.

### The parts · It fed the family, which is why it wasn't waiting
The fees were his living for that decade; writing wasn't a pastime, it was the profession. The distinction matters: once something actually supports you, you treat it differently, and it stops being an interval before going back.
e.g. Treat what you do in this stretch as a job — someone paying, a deadline. That's what makes it hold you.

### Q: How do I use it today?
Where you are: you've been pushed out of the centre, nobody asks your view, and you don't know how long this lasts.
Ask first: what did I deliver today? Does anyone pay for it, does it have a deadline? Have I arranged something physical?
Where it goes wrong: reading it as 'endure and you'll be back' — he spent no day enduring, he produced, and he might well never have gone back; and don't romanticise the wall. It was hard labour he set himself, not a pose.

### Lines to keep
Someone with output needn't wait for an invitation to feel present.
Being sidelined traps you in an argument. Sweat pulls you out.
Once a thing actually feeds you, it stops being an interval.

========================================================================
## Winston Churchill · Saying it and nobody listening
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/churchill/no-one-listened/
Source: His Commons speeches on German rearmament and the RAF, 1930s
Tags: Deep read, Winston Churchill, He put it in a form you could check

You see something others haven't, you say it, nobody listens. How he said it during those years.

### Q: What actually happened?
Through the thirties he made the same argument in Parliament: Germany is rearming and British air strength isn't keeping pace. Most of the House thought him bellicose and out of date, and his earlier record gave them reason to doubt his judgement. He didn't raise his voice. He collected figures on German aircraft production and read them out, again and again — things that could be checked. All of it went into the record: nobody listened at the time, and it stayed there.

### The parts · If nobody listens, change the form to a checkable one
An emotional judgement can't be verified, so it can't be refuted or confirmed either; saying it ten times equals saying it once. Numbers, dates and specific comparisons can be ignored today and reconciled later. A checkable sentence has a lifespan. A lament doesn't.
e.g. Rewrite the judgement nobody heard as something testable: which figure, by when, compared with what.

### The parts · Leaving a record matters more than convincing the room
He couldn't shift the majority, and he did get his judgement on the record with a date on it. The value of a judgement often isn't realised the day it's spoken but on the day someone reconciles the books. Without a record you can be right the whole time and unable to show it.
e.g. Write important judgements down and keep them dated. That's your only evidence later.

### The parts · What sidelined people should fear is softening the line
After long enough in the cold, people want to say something comfortable and buy back a little standing. He didn't. When he was called back it was precisely because he hadn't altered a word in ten years. Someone who has shifted isn't remembered when judgement is needed.
e.g. Don't revise the conclusion to buy agreement — unless there's a new fact, which is a different thing.

### Q: How do I use it today?
Where you are: you can see something others aren't taking seriously, you've said it repeatedly, and you're wondering whether to keep saying it.
Ask first: can I rewrite this as a checkable sentence? Have I recorded it with a date? Have I quietly softened it to be easier?
Where it goes wrong: reading it as 'stick to your view and you'll be vindicated' — he was wrong plenty of times. This is about the form, not the confidence; and correcting yourself on new facts is not the same as changing your line.

### Lines to keep
A checkable sentence has a lifespan. A lament doesn't.
Judgements pay out not when spoken but when someone checks the books.
Someone who shifted isn't remembered when judgement is needed.

========================================================================
## Winston Churchill · The year he turned sixty-five
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/churchill/sixty-five/
Source: Return to the Admiralty, September 1939; Prime Minister, 10 May 1940; The Gathering Storm
Tags: Deep read, Winston Churchill, The call came a decade later

You've been accumulating a long time with no way out in sight. What the day he was waiting for actually required.

### Q: What actually happened?
War broke out in September 1939 and he returned to the Admiralty. On 10 May 1940 he became Prime Minister, aged sixty-five. Writing later about that night, he described feeling as though his whole past life had been a preparation for this hour. The books written in the wilderness, the speeches on the record, the arguments rehearsed until fluent — all of it spent at once. He wasn't remembered. He was the one man who hadn't changed his line in ten years.

### The parts · When the moment comes, it takes what's already in your hands
Nobody had time to develop anyone. He wasn't called because he had become likeable, but because on this subject he alone had a ready judgement, a ready record and a ready way of putting it. Being prepared means having it when someone else is in a hurry.
e.g. Ask: if someone needed it tomorrow, what could I hand over as it stands?

### The parts · Sixty-five says the ledger isn't kept in years
By the standards of the day that was retirement age. What decided the matter was never the number of years but whether what he had built in that decade still existed and was still needed. Age only becomes the problem when your hands are empty.
e.g. Don't use age as the test. Count what's in your hands. That list decides whether you're still in time.

### The parts · What you accumulate rarely gets used where you expected
He wrote to feed his family, laid brick to spend himself, and gathered figures for speeches nobody listened to. None of it was for the day that came, and all of it was spent on it. While accumulating you can't know where it lands. You can only make sure it's real.
e.g. It's fine that what you're doing has no visible use. Make sure it's a real craft and not just passing time.

### Q: How do I use it today?
Where you are: you've been building for a long time with no exit in sight, doubting whether any of it is still worth anything, or whether you're past the age.
Ask first: if someone needed it tomorrow, what could I hand over as it stands? Is what I've built a real craft? Are my judgements on the record with dates?
Where it goes wrong: reading it as 'hold on and your day comes' — most people's doesn't, and his had specific conditions: something ready, and a line he hadn't altered. It is not a licence to stop acting.

### Lines to keep
Being prepared means having it when somebody else is in a hurry.
Age is only the problem when your hands are empty.
You can't know where it lands. You can make sure it's real.

========================================================================
## C.S. Lewis · Nobody told me grief felt like fear
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/cs-lewis/grief-feels-like-fear/
Source: C.S. Lewis, A Grief Observed, 1961
Tags: Deep read, C.S. Lewis, A Grief Observed

What the feeling actually is when you've just lost someone. Why Lewis called it fear, and what that's for.

### Q: What actually happened?
After his wife died, Lewis began recording his own state in exercise books. The first line is the famous one: "No one ever told me that grief felt so like fear" — not like sadness, like fear. What he describes is physical: the churn in the stomach, the inability to sit still, the constant swallowing, as though waiting for bad news. He notes another thing nobody warned him of: grief makes you idle. He wasn't analysing. He was finding that everything ever said about grief had left out the concrete parts.

### The parts · Name it correctly and you know how to treat it
He had always assumed grief was sadness, an emotion, and found it closer to fear, which is bodily. Get the name wrong and you reach for the wrong method — sadness is met by thinking it through, fear by letting the body settle. Give it the accurate name first.
e.g. If your stomach is churning and you can't sit down, that's fear. Settle the body before trying to think it through.

### The parts · The idleness is part of it, not a fault of yours
He wrote about not wanting to do anything, putting off the simplest tasks. He didn't take it as evidence he'd collapsed; he recorded it as a symptom. Knowing it comes with the territory saves you carrying a second load called 'why am I so useless'.
e.g. Wanting to do nothing in that stretch is ordinary. Don't add a charge of laziness on top of the grief.

### The parts · Writing it down keeps it from swallowing you whole
He wrote daily, and what he wrote was that day's state, not conclusions. In the moment of writing a person moves from being inside the grief to watching it, even for a few minutes. Those minutes are where you breathe.
e.g. Three lines a day on how today was. No reasoning needed — 'stomach still churning' will do.

### Q: How do I use it today?
Where you are: you've just lost someone who mattered, life doesn't join up, and you can't say what state you're in.
Ask first: does this feel more like sadness or more like fear? Have I been counting 'I don't want to do anything' as my own failing? Could I write three lines about today?
Where it goes wrong: reading it as 'grief has standard stages, follow them' — he later said grief isn't a process but a road where every bend looks like the end and isn't. This is about recognising it, not scheduling it.

### Lines to keep
Not like sadness. Like fear.
Sadness is met by thinking it through. Fear, by settling the body.
Writing it down moves you from inside the grief to watching it.

========================================================================
## C.S. Lewis · My faith turned out to be a house of cards
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/cs-lewis/house-of-cards/
Source: C.S. Lewis, A Grief Observed, 1961
Tags: Deep read, C.S. Lewis, You find out when it's knocked down

What held you up your whole life didn't hold this time. What Lewis wrote when he found that out about himself.

### Q: What actually happened?
Lewis was among the most famous Christian writers of his day, the author of many books arguing people into belief. After his wife died he found that what he had been saying for decades didn't work on him. You never know how much you believe something, he wrote, until its truth or falsehood becomes a matter of life and death. He didn't rush to patch it. He admitted it: the house had been made of cards, and nobody had ever pushed it. What happened, he later said, was not that faith was taken away. It was tested for the first time.

### The parts · A belief never tested may not be a belief
Everything he had argued for decades held in good weather and collapsed at the first real event. That doesn't prove the argument wrong; it proves it had never carried weight. Most of what people assume will hold them has never been loaded. The first loading is when you find out.
e.g. 'I'm quite philosophical about these things' doesn't count as evidence until after something happens.

### The parts · Don't rebuild immediately
He didn't find a new set of ideas to plug the hole. He let the hole sit for a while. People who rebuild in a hurry generally build the same house out of the same cards. Wait and see what is still standing afterwards — that is the actual foundation.
e.g. When the story that held you stops working, don't swap in another. Look at what's still upright.

### The parts · 'Tested' and 'taken away' are different things
At first he thought something had been taken from him. He later changed the word to tested. Same experience: the first phrasing makes you a victim, the second makes you someone finding out what's true. Only the second can be walked forward from.
e.g. 'I lost it' and 'I found out for the first time how much of it there was' — take the second.

### Q: How do I use it today?
Where you are: the thing that always held you — a belief, a way of seeing things — didn't hold this time, and you feel you have nothing.
Ask first: had it ever carried weight before? What's still standing after the collapse? Can I say 'tested' instead of 'taken away'?
Where it goes wrong: reading it as 'everything anyone believes is false' — he didn't abandon his faith, he exchanged it for one not made of cards. This is about testing, not denial.

### Lines to keep
You don't know how much you believe something until it's life or death.
Rebuild in a hurry and you use the same cards again.
'I lost it' or 'I found out how much there was'. Take the second.

========================================================================
## C.S. Lewis · I'm afraid of replacing her with my memory of her
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/cs-lewis/not-replacing-her/
Source: C.S. Lewis, A Grief Observed, 1961
Tags: Deep read, C.S. Lewis, The harder you grip, the more it warps

You're afraid time will erase them. Lewis found the opposite problem, and it frightened him more.

### Q: What actually happened?
Lewis quickly noticed something that alarmed him: the harder he tried to remember his wife, the more the person in his head warped — into someone gentler, more agreeable, closer to what he wanted, with all her real sharpness sanded away. That, he said, was worse than forgetting: not losing her, but replacing her with someone he had made. Then one day, when he had stopped trying, she came back clearly, as herself. Grip harder and it warps faster. Let go and the real one returns.

### The parts · What you deliberately preserve becomes the version you want
Memory isn't a recording; every replay rewrites it. Straining to remember someone is rewriting them to your own requirements — deleting what was uncomfortable, enlarging what you wanted. What's left is an agreeable statue, not the person.
e.g. Rehearse only someone's good qualities long enough and only good qualities remain. That isn't them any more.

### The parts · The fear of forgetting is what speeds the warping
The more you fear losing them the harder you grip, and the harder you grip the more it deforms. He found that after he let go she returned — because he was no longer manufacturing her; the memory surfaced on its own. Real things don't need holding in place.
e.g. Don't set out to think of them daily. What surfaces on its own is the one that's actually them.

### The parts · Keeping their sharpness is how you keep them
He treasured his wife's least agreeable qualities — the bluntness, the appetite for argument, the refusal to be polite — because those are the parts he could not have invented. What irritates you about a person is the evidence they weren't your imagination.
e.g. Remember the two or three things that annoyed you. They resemble the person more than the virtues do.

### Q: How do I use it today?
Where you are: someone important is gone and you're afraid time will take them, so you rehearse them every day.
Ask first: is the person I'm holding gentler and more perfect than the real one? Can I still name the things about them that bothered me?
Where it goes wrong: hearing it as 'don't think about them' — he didn't stop thinking, he stopped straining; and don't turn 'keep the sharpness' into remembering only the bad, which is another rewrite.

### Lines to keep
The harder he tried to remember her, the more she warped.
Grip harder and it warps faster. Let go and the real one returns.
The things that annoyed you resemble them more than the virtues do.

========================================================================
## Marie Curie · She took over his course
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/curie/the-lecture/
Source: Pierre Curie died April 1906; her first Sorbonne lecture, 5 November 1906
Tags: Deep read, Marie Curie, Starting where he stopped

The person who mattered most is suddenly gone and the days still have to continue. What she did seven months later.

### Q: What actually happened?
On 19 April 1906 Pierre Curie was knocked down by a horse-drawn wagon in a Paris street and killed instantly. The Sorbonne gave his chair to his widow. On 5 November she gave her first lecture, with the room overflowing and journalists present, everyone waiting to hear her say something about him. She offered no eulogy. She opened at the point where her husband's last lecture had stopped, and continued. She became the first woman to hold a professorship there.

### The parts · Catch hold of one specific thing that must be done
An enormous blank can't be faced directly. What can be faced is something with a time, a place and a content: two o'clock, that room, that course. It doesn't solve the grief. It gives the day a shape you can put yourself inside.
e.g. For the next few days, fix one thing that has to be done and has an hour and a place attached.

### The parts · Continuing looks more like keeping faith than a farewell
Everyone was waiting for a leave-taking; she carried on. She didn't turn the lecture into a ceremony, she finished the passage he hadn't finished. The most concrete way to commemorate someone is often to keep doing the thing they had in hand.
e.g. If you want to do something for someone who has gone, look for the unfinished thing you could take on.

### The parts · When people are waiting for a performance, you may just work
The crowd had come to see a widow's grief. She didn't provide it. Nobody in the worst of it is obliged to bring their pain out for viewing; finishing the work in front of you is a complete account of yourself.
e.g. If you don't want to speak, don't. Finish what's in your hands. You owe nobody a performance.

### Q: How do I use it today?
Where you are: the most important person has just gone, life has to continue, and you don't know which step is first.
Ask first: is there one thing in the next few days that has to be done, at a set hour in a set place? Is there something of theirs I could take on? Am I forcing myself to give someone else an account?
Where it goes wrong: hearing 'keep busy and it stops hurting' — in the same period she was writing a grief journal, lecturing by day and speaking to him at night. Work is not a way round mourning.

### Lines to keep
It doesn't solve the grief. It gives the day a shape.
The most concrete memorial is to continue the thing they had in hand.
Nobody at their worst owes anyone a performance of it.

## Marie Curie · A notebook written to the dead
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/curie/journal-of-grief/
Source: Marie Curie's private notebook to Pierre, 1906–07, published after her death
Tags: Deep read, Marie Curie, What you can't say aloud, write to him

There are things you cannot say to a living person. Where those go. What she put in the notebook that year.

### Q: What actually happened?
For more than a year after Pierre's death she wrote in a notebook. Not a diary — words addressed to him: where she had been, what the children said, how she couldn't bear it, what she was supposed to do without him. The sentences are full of 'you'. She never showed it to anyone in her lifetime. After a year or so the entries thinned, and nowhere in it does she write that she needs to move on.

### The parts · Write it to that person, not to anyone else
Said to the living it becomes a request for comfort; said to yourself it becomes analysis. Only addressed to them does the true thing come out — the undignified, unreasonable, repetitive parts. Who the letter is to decides what you can write.
e.g. Write their name at the top and use 'you'. Don't make it a record that someone else could read.

### The parts · Mourning isn't a process due to finish
She set no deadline and never wrote that it was time to turn the page. The entries thinned by themselves; nothing was completed. Treat grief as a task with an end date and you spend it grieving and blaming yourself for still grieving.
e.g. Don't set a date by which you should be better. The day the writing thins will arrive on its own.

### The parts · Nobody was going to read it, which is why it's honest
She kept it private for life. Precisely because it was for no one, she didn't have to be presentable, or reasonable, or brave. A notebook addressed only to the dead is one of the few places the living can be completely unperformed.
e.g. Find somewhere you're certain nobody will look. Not performing is the only requirement.

### Q: How do I use it today?
Where you are: there are things you can't say to anyone, and saying them gets you either comfort or advice, both of which make it worse.
Ask first: who are these words actually addressed to? Could I just write to them? Am I setting myself a date to be better by?
Where it goes wrong: reading it as 'writing makes you feel better' — she wrote for over a year and it didn't. This is about finding a place where the unsayable can be said honestly, not a treatment.

### Lines to keep
Who the letter is addressed to decides what you can write.
Treat grief as a task with a deadline and you'll blame yourself too.
A notebook for the dead is where the living need not perform.

## Marie Curie · The little Curies
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/curie/the-little-curies/
Source: The mobile radiography units she organised during the First World War
Tags: Deep read, Marie Curie, Put the skill where it's needed now

Your skill and what's in front of you don't match. Where she put hers when the war started.

### Q: What actually happened?
When war broke out, wounded men had to be carried far behind the lines before they could be X-rayed, and many didn't survive the journey. She left the laboratory, raised money, had vehicles converted with generators and X-ray equipment, learned to drive and to repair the cars herself, and took them near the front with her teenage daughter Irène. The soldiers called them the little Curies. She published almost nothing during those years.

### The parts · Point the craft at what's needed here
Her field was research, and what was scarce then was not a new discovery but getting a wounded man photographed today. A craft is only settled inside a specific situation, and situations change. What your field is matters less than what's missing now.
e.g. Ask: what specific thing in front of me needs this skill most right now?

### The parts · She didn't wait for a role worthy of her. She learned to drive
With her standing she could have lent her name and nothing else. What she learned instead was driving and vehicle repair — work with no status in it. Getting anything actually done always contains a stretch of unglamorous work nobody gets to skip.
e.g. To get something done, take on the least prestigious part of it first.

### The parts · Years with no output aren't wasted years
Academically those years are nearly blank. Counted in papers, they were squandered. Counted in people who lived, they weren't. You have to decide yourself which ledger your life settles in, or you will live by somebody else's standard.
e.g. Before judging a stretch of time, decide what the ledger is: output, usefulness, or something else.

### Q: How do I use it today?
Where you are: you have real skills and what's in front of you can't use them, or the work that could looks beneath you.
Ask first: what specific thing most needs this skill now? Will I take the least prestigious part of it? What ledger am I settling these years in?
Where it goes wrong: hearing it as 'your field doesn't matter' — what she did was directly related to her expertise, just used differently; and setting it down was temporary. She went back to the laboratory after the war.

### Lines to keep
A craft is only settled inside a situation, and situations change.
Getting anything done contains a stretch with no status in it.
Decide what ledger you settle in, or you live by someone else's.

## Carol Dweck · Praise the process, not the talent
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/dweck/praise-the-process/
Source: Mindset; the praise experiments
Tags: Deep read, Carol Dweck, Praising cleverness makes people avoid challenge

One sentence of praise changes what a child picks next. This piece is about where the change happens.

### Q: What actually happened?
After a set of problems she gave students one of two kinds of praise: one group heard 'you're so clever', the other 'you worked hard'. Offered a choice of the next set, the ones praised for cleverness took the easier one more often, the ones praised for effort took the harder one. Her reading: praise for talent makes people avoid challenge; praise for process makes them accept it. Talent praise turns results into proof of talent, so every later challenge becomes a threat to the self. The watershed is the moment of failure — information in one mindset, verdict in the other.

### The parts · Praise the specific move, not the label
'You're clever' is a label, and labels need protecting. 'You went back through every wrong answer' is a move, and moves can be repeated. The test is simple: can they do this praise again next time?
e.g. They did well: ask how they prepared. Don't say they've got a good brain. The first is repeatable, the second can only be defended.

### The parts · The moment of failure decides the direction
In good weather the two mindsets look identical. The watershed is the instant something fails: one reads it as 'I can't', the other as 'that approach can't'. The difference isn't the intensity of the feeling. It's whether they go looking for the cause.
e.g. A rejected proposal: the person who asks 'which part doesn't hold' fixes it. The one who decides they're not suited never proposes again.

### The parts · The word 'yet'
Replacing 'failed' with 'not yet passed' turns a result into a point in time. The small change works because it moves attention from what level I am to where I've got to.
e.g. Change 'I can't write' to 'I can't write yet'. One word decides whether the next sentence looks for a method or an excuse.

### Q: How do I use it today?
Where you are: giving feedback to a child or a report.
Ask first: is this praising talent or a specific move? Could they do it again next time?
Where it goes wrong: turning process praise into a mechanical formula and never mentioning a genuinely good result — that reads as being fobbed off.

### Lines to keep
Praise for talent makes people avoid challenge. Praise for process doesn't.
In a growth mindset failure is information. In a fixed one it's a verdict.
Use 'not yet' instead of 'can't'.

========================================================================
## Carol Dweck · The effect is much smaller than the popular story
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/dweck/effect-size/
Source: Large-scale replications in recent years; corrections to the original claims
Tags: Deep read, Carol Dweck, The boundary worth drawing

The concept got told as a master key. This piece is about how big it actually is.

### Q: What actually happened?
This layer has to be said plainly: large-scale replications in recent years find the effect of mindset interventions far smaller than the original book conveyed, close to zero in some populations, with the clearer benefits concentrated among disadvantaged students. That doesn't overturn the concept. It overturns the reading that a change of attitude changes everything. It's a real but mild factor, not the switch that decides outcomes. Treating it as a master key means ignoring resources, teaching, foundations and rest — all heavier variables — and putting the whole responsibility on the person's attitude.

### The parts · Mild and real, not a switch
The effect exists and its magnitude is far below the popular story. The correct use is as one improvable factor among many, not the main explanation for success or failure.
e.g. A child struggling: look at teaching, foundations and sleep before attributing it to the wrong attitude.

### The parts · Blaming attitude is the easiest and least fair move
'You just don't believe in yourself enough' converts a systemic difficulty into a defect of character. It is particularly unfair to people short of resources — what they lack is usually not belief.
e.g. Telling an unsupported student to have a growth mindset says the difficulty is something they imagined.

### The parts · Knowing the boundary is what makes it usable
Once you admit the effect is mild the concept becomes more usable: it's worth the cost of one sentence — change how you praise, add the word 'yet' — and not worth a training programme and slogans on the wall.
e.g. Changing your own wording is cheap. Spending heavily on mindset training and expecting results will disappoint.

### Q: How do I use it today?
Where you are: someone is explaining a result as a problem of attitude.
Ask first: have the heavier variables — method, resources, foundations, rest — been checked? If not, attitude is the laziest and least accurate attribution available.
Where it goes wrong: dropping it entirely because the effect is mild. Changing how you praise costs almost nothing and is still worth doing.

### Lines to keep
Replications find the effect far smaller than the book conveyed.
The clearer benefits are concentrated among disadvantaged students.
Treat it as a master key and you'll ignore the heavier variables.

========================================================================
## Excellent Sheep · Good at hurdles, bad at choosing a road
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/excellent-sheep/hurdles/
Source: Excellent Sheep
Tags: Deep read, Excellent Sheep, Two completely different abilities

Why people who succeeded at every stage go blank the moment the standards stop. What they never practised.

### Q: What actually happened?
Deresiewicz taught at Yale for ten years and sat on admissions. What he saw was young people extraordinarily good at clearing set hurdles — grades, competitions, internships, the CV — and unable to say what they wanted. They were superb at clearing hurdles and could not tell you where they were going. His typical scene: an outstanding student who has no idea why she chose the subject, only that she had to be best at it. He insists this isn't a personal failing. Someone optimised since childhood to meet every standard has never once practised deciding what matters.

### The parts · The two abilities don't substitute
'Be the best at this' and 'decide what's worth doing' are different skills. The first is drilled constantly inside any evaluation system. The second can only be trained where there is no correct answer — so the smoother the run, the likelier the second is blank.
e.g. The drop from star student to lost graduate usually isn't about ability. It's the first time nobody set the standard.

### The parts · Never having failed makes failure unimaginable
The price of an unbroken run is no experience of failing, so failure gets imagined as catastrophic. The result is avoiding anything you might not be good at, and a range that narrows year by year.
e.g. Not switching to the thing you actually want because 'I've built up experience here.' The real reason is being a beginner again.

### The parts · The target is the system, not the students
The book reads easily as blaming young people for lacking independence. The author's subject is the filtering machinery that trains them this way — every step rational, and the sum a life with no direction.
e.g. Fine for self-examination, useless as a lecture. Who set the hurdles and who benefits is the real question.

### Q: How do I use it today?
Where you are: you know exactly what counts as doing well, and can't answer what you want.
Ask first: is this choice what I want, or is it simply the next hurdle? When did I last do something with no standard attached?
Where it goes wrong: using it to write off effort and achievement. The problem isn't being excellent. It's only being excellent.

### Lines to keep
Superb at clearing hurdles, and unable to say where they were going.
Never allowed to fail, you imagine failure as unsurvivable.
Every step rational, and the sum is a life with no direction.

## Excellent Sheep · Give yourself time with no scoreboard
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/excellent-sheep/no-scoreboard/
Source: Excellent Sheep
Tags: Deep read, Excellent Sheep, Any standard becomes a thing to optimise

How to find out what you actually want. The condition that has to be true first.

### Q: What actually happened?
Deresiewicz's prescription isn't a new major or a new job. It's a stretch of time with no evaluation attached — doing one thing that isn't scored, for long enough. The reasoning is direct: only when nobody is grading you do you find out what you actually want. Where a standard exists, people optimise it automatically, and the optimising drowns out the signal about whether you want to do this at all. The problem isn't that you can't think it through. It's that no environment lets the question surface.

### The parts · A score existing means you'll chase it
This isn't weak will, it's the default. Wherever there's a comparable metric, attention slides to it. So answering 'what do I want' requires temporarily leaving the places that have metrics.
e.g. A hobby starts taking commissions and counting followers, and quickly becomes a second job. Not corruption — a score.

### The parts · It only works if it's long enough
A few days tests novelty. The signal that counts is whether you still want to continue after the novelty has gone and it's got a bit boring. He's describing months, not a couple of weekends.
e.g. Six months on something nobody is watching produces better judgement than any careers course.

### The parts · Separate 'I want this' from 'this is the next hurdle'
This is the usable daily test. Facing an opportunity, ask whether what draws you is the content itself or the fact that it's the obvious next step on the current track. The second disguises itself very well as the first.
e.g. A promotion on the table: separate wanting the work from not wanting to look like you've stalled.

### Q: How do I use it today?
Where you are: you're making a choice about direction.
Ask first: is it the content that draws me, or is it simply the next hurdle? Have I done anything unscored lately?
Where it goes wrong: reading it as a reason to quit and wander. He's describing carving out an unscored space, not demolishing the structure.

### Lines to keep
Only when nobody is grading you do you find out what you want.
Wherever a comparable metric exists, attention slides to it.
Still willing after the novelty is gone — that's the signal.

========================================================================
## Fan Li · In a drought, stock boats
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/fan-li/stock-the-opposite/
Source: Records of the Grand Historian, Biographies of the Money-Makers
Tags: Deep read, Fan Li, Buy it when nobody wants it

When is a thing cheapest? At the moment everybody agrees it is useless.

### Q: What actually happened?
Among the strategies Fan Li's teacher gave the state of Yue is one very simple rule: in drought, stock boats; in flood, stock carts; and so be ready for the shortage. In a drought nobody wants a boat and the price is lowest; after drought comes flood, and then a boat is dearest. He generalised it into a law of price: examine surplus and shortage and you know dear from cheap. What is dear to the extreme turns down; what is cheap to the extreme turns up. So sell the dear as if it were dung, and take the cheap as if it were pearls.

### The parts · Buy when the demand has gone
Price is set by present demand; value by future demand. The entire difficulty of this rule is that at the moment of buying, every visible piece of evidence says the thing is worthless. A decision with no evidence behind it is exactly what the method requires.
e.g. Hiring during layoffs, signing long deals at the coldest point, starting a project nobody works on — each done without any external confirmation.

### The parts · The cycle is the premise. Not everything comes back
Drought and flood alternate, which is what makes stocking boats correct. If a decline is structural and won't return, buying cheap is catching a falling knife. Before using the rule you have to judge: is this a cycle or an ending?
e.g. Capacity at the bottom of a cycle is worth buying. Capacity replaced by a technology isn't, at any price. Today the two price curves look identical.

### The parts · Money has to keep moving
There's a line of his that gets skipped: money should flow like water. What you stockpile is goods, not capital. Locking your funds in one place to wait for an appreciation is no different from burying them in the ground.
e.g. Everything pressed into one appreciating asset means that even when the call is right, you lost every option in between.

### Q: How do I use it today?
Where you are: something is cheap right now and everyone says it has no future.
Ask first: is it cheap because the cycle is at a low, or because it has genuinely been replaced?
Where it goes wrong: bottom-fishing a structural decline as though it were a cyclical low; or being right and still locking every last resource inside it.

### Lines to keep
In drought, stock boats. In flood, stock carts.
Sell the dear like dung. Take the cheap like pearls.
Money should keep moving, like water.

========================================================================
## Fan Li · Long neck, beak like a bird
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/fan-li/leave-at-the-top/
Source: Records of the Grand Historian, House of Goujian; Biographies of the Money-Makers
Tags: Deep read, Fan Li, Read the ending off the person

He left the moment Yue destroyed Wu, at the highest point. What he was reading when he decided.

### Q: What actually happened?
With Wu destroyed, Fan Li left at once and took a boat onto the lakes. He wrote to Wen Zhong, who stayed, and his reasoning was not about the situation but about the man: the king of Yue has a long neck and a beak like a bird's; you can share hardship with him, you cannot share ease. Wen Zhong stayed, and was later ordered to kill himself. Fan Li changed his name, went into trade in Qi, made a vast fortune, was offered the chancellorship, returned the seal, gave the fortune away, started again at Tao, and made and dispersed a fortune three times.

### The parts · Reading the person beats reading the situation
Situations change; a person's construction doesn't. Fan Li's judgement wasn't 'this is dangerous now' but 'here is what this man becomes when things go well' — a judgement that already held before Wu fell. It was just not yet needed.
e.g. How a partner behaves when money is short tells you nothing about how he behaves when it's divided. Watch how he treats people below him while he's winning.

### The parts · Sharing hardship and sharing ease are different capacities
The precision is in separating two relationships. People who carried something together can't necessarily divide something together. The first is held by a common enemy; the second demands restraint in dividing gains — far rarer, and only visible after the win.
e.g. Teams that were fiercely united while building often break at the first real payout. The people didn't change. The test did.

### The parts · Letting go is harder than accumulating
He built a great fortune three times and gave it away three times. This wasn't a performance of generosity — returning the chancellor's seal in Qi, starting again at Tao, each time he abandoned a position already in hand. Many can accumulate. Almost nobody puts down what they already hold.
e.g. Handing over the business you built to start an uncertain line is far harder than minding the mature one, even though everyone knows it will decline.

### Q: How do I use it today?
Where you are: something big has just succeeded and you're weighing what position comes next.
Ask first: the people who did this with me — what are they like at the dividing stage? Have I seen it?
Where it goes wrong: reading only whether the situation is favourable and never the construction of the people; or treating letting go as a posture while actually releasing nothing.

### Lines to keep
You can share hardship with him. You cannot share ease.
Three times he made a fortune, and three times gave it away.
The construction of a person doesn't change. The situation does.

========================================================================
## John Gottman · The four horsemen
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/gottman/four-horsemen/
Source: The Gottman marriage lab; The Seven Principles for Making Marriage Work
Tags: Deep read, John Gottman, Four signals that predict a breakup

He watches fifteen minutes of one argument. This piece is about what he is actually watching.

### Q: What actually happened?
Gottman recorded thousands of couples talking, coded expression, tone and heart rate frame by frame, then tracked who divorced years later. What predicted a breakup wasn't how fiercely they fought but whether four signals appeared, which he called the four horsemen: criticism (attacking the person, not the act), contempt (sarcasm, eye-rolling), defensiveness (returning the blame) and stonewalling (shutting the other out). The single strongest predictor of divorce is contempt — and the research found it affects the recipient's immune function.

### The parts · Criticism and complaint are different things
A complaint targets behaviour: you didn't do the washing up and I'm exhausted. Criticism targets character: you're just lazy. The first can be solved; the second can only be defended. Many people think they're raising an issue while every sentence defines the other person, and so the same problem runs ten years.
e.g. Swap 'you never deal with the kids' for 'I did all three pickups this week'. Same event, and the second can be caught.

### The parts · Contempt is a slow poison, not venting
Eye-rolling, mockery, mimicking their tone — all of it says I am above you. It differs from anger: anger is about the event, contempt says the person is unworthy. It's the strongest single predictor in his data because it destroys the foundation, not one conversation.
e.g. 'What would you know' and 'fine, you're always right' need correcting on the spot. That isn't arguing, it's demolition.

### The parts · Defensiveness returns the ball, it doesn't clarify
'I've been busy, and so have you' looks like explaining and is a counter-attack. Its function is to refuse any share of responsibility, and once both sides are defending, the conversation becomes mutual evidence and never reaches a solution.
e.g. When the pickups come up, take the part you can admit — 'you did do all three' — before explaining your side.

### Q: How do I use it today?
Where you are: the same thing gets fought about and every round escalates.
Ask first: was that last sentence about the event or about the person? Any sarcasm or eye-rolling? Am I explaining or returning the ball?
Where it goes wrong: using the four horsemen to charge the other person — 'that's contempt' is itself an attack. It's a checklist for yourself, not a verdict.

### Lines to keep
The strongest single predictor of divorce is contempt.
Criticism targets the person. A complaint targets the act.
The more often the four appear, the likelier the breakup.

========================================================================
## John Gottman · Repair attempts
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/gottman/repair-attempts/
Source: The Gottman marriage lab
Tags: Deep read, John Gottman, Whether you fight matters less than whether you stop

Healthy relationships argue fiercely too. So where do they differ from the ones that break.

### Q: What actually happened?
One of Gottman's counterintuitive findings: happy couples aren't the ones who don't fight, they're the ones who repair while fighting. He called the move of reaching for the brake mid-escalation a repair attempt — a joke, an offered way out, a 'wait, we've gone off topic'. In stable relationships repair attempts succeed more often, and not because the technique is better: because the other person is willing to take it. That willingness depends on the balance built up beforehand. He put a number on it — in stable relationships positive interactions run about five to one against negative.

### The parts · Repair succeeds or fails on the ordinary days
The same joke defuses things in a relationship with a healthy balance and reads as not taking it seriously in one that's overdrawn. So what decides whether a conflict can be stopped is the unremarkable responses, presence and small concessions of the past weeks. Technique in the moment mostly fails.
e.g. 'Let's not fight' after three months of silence rarely works. What would have worked is what wasn't done in those three months.

### The parts · Taking the offered way out is harder than offering it
Offering it risks being refused; taking it means giving up winning this round. Most relationships stick on the second: they heard it, and 'why should I be the one to let it go' stops them. Insisting on winning wins the round and loses the relationship.
e.g. 'Have we gone a bit far?' — answering 'yeah, a bit' is worth more than another round of evidence.

### The parts · Five to one is a balance, not a formula
The ratio gets misused as licence to say one cruel thing per five kind ones. Gottman means the everyday texture of the relationship should be mostly positive, not that praise offsets attacks. An attack costs far more than praise pays — that's why the ratio is lopsided.
e.g. Use it as a check: over the past week, was the texture between us warm or cold? Not 'have I complimented them five times'.

### Q: How do I use it today?
Where you are: mid-argument, both waiting for the other to give way first.
Ask first: did they offer a way out that I didn't take? Is our balance healthy enough to cover this overdraft?
Where it goes wrong: making repair something the same person always does. That isn't repair, it's one-sided depletion.

### Lines to keep
Happy couples aren't the ones who don't fight. They repair.
In stable relationships, positives run about five to one.
Whether a repair works depends on the account built beforehand.

========================================================================
## Mark Granovetter · The strength of weak ties
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/granovetter/weak-ties/
Source: Granovetter, The Strength of Weak Ties, AJS, 1973
Tags: Deep read, Mark Granovetter, Opportunity arrives from people you rarely see

Who to ask when you're looking for work. Your instinct gives the wrong answer; here's what the data gave.

### Q: What actually happened?
In 1973 Granovetter surveyed 282 people about how they found their jobs. Among those who got there through a personal contact, 56% said they saw that person only occasionally, and 28% said rarely — the people who mattered were the ones they barely knew. That runs against instinct: your closest friends want to help you most. But the reason isn't willingness, it's information. Your circles overlap almost completely with your closest friends'; someone you rarely see is standing in a different network.

### The parts · What matters isn't willingness, it's whether the news is new
Close friends are more willing to help and hold almost the same information you do — same people, same news. A weak tie is not more generous. He is standing somewhere else, holding the part you can't reach from where you are.
e.g. You already knew about the opening in the team chat. The genuinely new thing comes from the person you see once a year.

### The parts · So maintain breadth, not depth
This changes where the effort goes: rather than pouring all of it into a few people, keep more weak ties in the 'still knows who you are' state. The cost is tiny — an occasional message, a hello with no request attached — and that's enough to keep the line usable.
e.g. Contacting old colleagues only once you want to move is usually too late. That line has to be kept while you don't need it.

### The parts · When you move, weak ties are what breaks first
Change city or leave an industry and what disappears isn't the close friends — those survive — it's the wide band of people you saw occasionally. That's exactly the layer that supplies new opportunities, so the drought after a move isn't imagined. It's structural.
e.g. Six months in a new city and nothing comes to you. You didn't get worse. That layer hasn't been built yet.

### Q: How do I use it today?
Where you are: you're looking for something — a job, a partner, customers — and circling the same few people.
Ask first: of everyone I've contacted in six months, how many do I see only a few times a year? If almost none, one whole source of opportunity is switched off.
Where it goes wrong: reading it as collect contacts — a weak tie only works if the person still knows who you are and what you do; and don't neglect close friends for this. That's a different loss.

### Lines to keep
Of people who found work through a contact, 56% saw them only occasionally.
Your closest friends want to help most. The useful news sits further out.
When you move, the layer that breaks first is the one that brought opportunities.

========================================================================
## Mark Granovetter · No strong tie is a bridge
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/granovetter/no-strong-tie-is-a-bridge/
Source: Granovetter 1973, on bridges
Tags: Deep read, Mark Granovetter, The people closest to you know what you know

It sounds like a turn of phrase. It's a structural result, and here is what it rests on.

### Q: What actually happened?
Granovetter states it flatly: no strong tie is a bridge. The reason isn't sentiment, it's geometry. If you're close to A and close to B, then A and B probably know each other — close people introduce each other, and the circle closes. Once it's closed, the three of you know largely the same things, and none of you is a route to anywhere outside. Only rarely-used ties can be bridges, because only they have non-overlapping networks at each end.

### The parts · Closure is what strong ties inevitably produce
This isn't a question of social strategy, it's geometry: closeness means frequent contact, and frequent contact makes your friends meet each other. Closure itself is good — it's where support and trust come from — but it also means information circulates rather than arrives.
e.g. A tight team is superbly informed internally and the slowest in the building to notice what's changing outside.

### The parts · To test whether a tie is a bridge, look at the overlap
The test is simple: if this person knows most of the people you know, he isn't a bridge; if you share very few mutual contacts, he probably is. A bridge's value has nothing to do with how close you are and everything to do with the overlap at each end.
e.g. The person you share two mutual friends with is likelier to bring you something new than the one you share thirty with.

### The parts · A group's health shows in how many bridges it has
Applied to a team: an organisation made entirely of strong ties is warm inside and slowest to react to anything outside. What needs protecting is the few people who don't quite fit in and spend time elsewhere. They are the bridges, and bridges are what cohesion squeezes out first.
e.g. The one who's always off with another department is usually the door news comes through.

### Q: How do I use it today?
Where you are: you want yourself or your team to hear sooner what's happening outside.
Ask first: how many lines do I have into circles that don't overlap with mine? Name them. If you can't name one, build a bridge before deepening what you already have.
Where it goes wrong: using this to dismiss close ties — they supply support and trust, a different job entirely; or setting out to 'network outward', which makes the tie a task, and those don't hold.

### Lines to keep
No strong tie is a bridge.
Close to A and close to B? A and B probably know each other.
Bridges are what a group squeezes out first when it wants cohesion.

========================================================================
## Han Feizi · Don't build a system that needs good people
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/han-feizi/not-counting-on-goodness/
Source: Han Feizi, Eminent Learning; The Five Vermin
Tags: Deep read, Han Feizi, Make the right move the cheap one

A system that only runs when people are conscientious hasn't started working yet. How to design rules that don't need it.

### Q: What actually happened?
Han Feizi puts it coldly: I do not count on people being good to me; I make it so they cannot do wrong. He offers an arithmetic. Wait for arrow shafts that straighten themselves and in a hundred generations you get no arrows; wait for wood that rounds itself and in a thousand you get no wheels. Yet everyone has arrows and wheels, because someone invented the jig that straightens them. His conclusion: government cannot wait for sages. It builds tools.

### The parts · Conscientiousness is scarce and can't be the foundation
Depending on people to be conscientious stakes the system's stability on its least controllable variable. His alternative is the jig — the tool that straightens timber. Rules don't exist to improve people. They exist so that ordinary people produce acceptable results.
e.g. 'Everyone please follow the style guide' won't converge in ten years. A linter converges it in a day. Not conscience — tooling.

### The parts · Make the right road the least effortful one
The practical version of 'make it so they cannot do wrong' is to build the non-compliant road so it costs more than the compliant one. If going round the process is faster than going through it, no amount of exhortation matters. People are choosing the cheaper path.
e.g. Expenses take five steps and three signatures, and paying yourself back later takes one. Somebody will pay themselves back later.

### The parts · Don't design for the rare case
The commonest misuse is constraining everyone to stop one or two. Han Feizi is describing universal tools, not patches aimed at individuals. The cost of a rule is borne by everybody and the benefit accrues against a few. That ledger rarely balances.
e.g. One faked claim, so now every claim needs three photos. The faker adapts; several hundred people lose two hours a month.

### Q: How do I use it today?
Where you are: the same class of problem keeps recurring and you've raised it many times.
Ask first: is the right road currently more effort than the wrong one?
Where it goes wrong: substituting announcements for tools; making everyone pay a cost in order to block a handful.

### Lines to keep
I do not count on people being good. I make wrong impossible.
Wait for arrows that straighten themselves and you get no arrows.
Rules don't make people better. They make ordinary work acceptable.

========================================================================
## Han Feizi · The two handles
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/han-feizi/two-handles/
Source: Han Feizi, The Two Handles
Tags: Deep read, Han Feizi, Reward and punishment can't be lent out

What power actually consists of. It turns out to be two things, and neither can be handed to anyone.

### Q: What actually happened?
Han Feizi states it like a definition: the ruler controls his ministers by two handles, and the two handles are punishment and favour. Killing is punishment; reward is favour. His example is the state of Qi, where the minister Tian Chang obtained ranks and stipends from the ruler to distribute to the officials, and lent grain by a large measure while collecting by a small one, putting the people in his debt. The ruler ended up hollow. His verdict: Tian Chang wasn't too strong. The ruler gave away the handle of favour.

### The parts · Power's substance is reward and consequence
Titles, grades and reporting lines are the form. What actually decides who listens to whom is who can grant good outcomes and who can bring bad ones. Everything else can be delegated; hand over these two and the seat is empty. The name remains and nobody is looking at you.
e.g. You're nominally in charge, and raises, promotions and ratings are decided elsewhere. The team aligns to the other person. That's structure, not loyalty.

### The parts · Lending them out is easy; taking them back is not
Once one person exercises reward and punishment for long enough, the organisation re-forms around them. Taking it back is no longer a question of authority — you face a network of dependence, and everyone who benefited will instinctively defend them.
e.g. One senior person has allocated resources for years. Moving them means moving everyone they lifted.

### The parts · Deliver both yourself
Letting someone else announce the good news and carrying the bad yourself sounds considerate. It gives away the favour and keeps the punishment. Han Feizi advises the opposite: both must come from you, or people only remember whoever handed them the good thing.
e.g. HR announces the raise and the manager delivers the criticism. Gratitude goes to the company, resentment to the manager.

### Q: How do I use it today?
Where you are: you're nominally responsible for something and can't move it.
Ask first: on this, who currently decides the good outcomes and the bad ones?
Where it goes wrong: delegating reward and punishment as though they were admin; letting others announce good news while you absorb the bad.

### Lines to keep
The ruler controls by two handles: punishment and favour.
A tiger masters a dog by claws. Lend them out and it reverses.
Everything else can be delegated. These two empty the seat.

========================================================================
## Han Feizi · Match the deed to the word
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/han-feizi/form-and-name/
Source: Han Feizi, The Way of the Ruler; The Two Handles
Tags: Deep read, Han Feizi, What was said, what was done

The hard part of review isn't setting standards. It's what you do when the standard and the facts disagree.

### Q: What actually happened?
