Han Feizi's method is matching form to name: the official states what he will accomplish (the name), and you check it against what was actually produced (the form). His extreme example: Marquis Zhao of Han fell asleep drunk, and the keeper of the hat, seeing him cold, covered him with a robe. On waking the marquis punished both the keeper of the robes and the keeper of the hat — one for neglect, one for overstepping. Overstepping is the worse harm, because it dissolves the boundary. The principle being established: your own words are the measure.

### The parts · The standard comes out of his mouth
Let the name define itself and the task define itself. Not a target imposed from above but a commitment stated by the person carrying it. At review there is then no arguing about whether the standard was reasonable — he set it. The only question left is whether it was met.
e.g. Rather than assigning a number, have them write what they will deliver this quarter and how it will be judged. Review only that page.

### The parts · Overshooting counts too
Form exceeding name is also pursued. Doing more looks good, and it means the judgement at commitment time was wrong, and it usually consumed someone else's resources. A system that punishes only shortfalls trains everyone to commit as low as possible.
e.g. Everyone sets targets at what they can certainly hit and exceeds them yearly. That organisation no longer knows its own capacity.

### The parts · Reconcile against the page agreed beforehand
If the ruler is chosen at review time, the whole thing becomes retroactive approval. Matching requires the name first and the form after, with no change in between. Change it once and the system reverts to personal favour.
e.g. Swap the criteria at quarter end, however reasonably, and nobody writes a serious commitment next quarter.

### Q: How do I use it today?
Where you are: it's review time and the two of you disagree on whether it counts as done.
Ask first: before this started, what standard did he write down himself?
Where it goes wrong: chasing only shortfalls and never overshoots, which pushes everyone to commit low; deciding which ruler to use only after the fact.

### Lines to keep
Let the name define itself, and the task define itself.
Deed fits the task and task fits the words: reward. Otherwise: punish.
Change the ruler at review and nobody writes a real commitment again.

========================================================================
## Harvard Study of Adult Development · Your relationships at 50 predict your body at 80
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/harvard-study/relationships-predict-health/
Source: Harvard Study of Adult Development, 1938–present; Robert Waldinger
Tags: Deep read, Harvard Study of Adult Development, More accurate than cholesterol

What actually decides how healthy you are late in life. What eighty years of tracking put in first place.

### Q: What actually happened?
In 1938 Harvard began following 268 sophomores, later adding 456 boys from Boston's poorest neighbourhoods. Every two years they asked how life was going; every five they ran medical exams. It is still running. Robert Waldinger, the fourth director, says the sturdiest finding in all of it is this: how satisfied you are with your close relationships at fifty predicts your health at eighty better than your cholesterol does. Not income. Not fame. Not class.

### The parts · It runs through the body
This one gets read as a greeting card, but it lands on hard measures: people in chronically strained relationships report more chronic pain in later life and show earlier memory decline. The researchers keep repeating that this isn't about mood. The body settles the bill.
e.g. The cohort who were professionally successful and personally isolated have visibly lower health curves in old age.

### The parts · A relationship that survives isn't the same as one that protects
There's an unwelcome line in the data: a long, high-conflict, mutually draining marriage does more damage to health than separating. What protects you is the quality inside it, not whether it's still standing. 'Staying for the kids' does not balance on this ledger.
e.g. Twenty years of holding it together, and both people's medical results are paying for it.

### The parts · The window to change it is later than most people assume
Most people decide after midlife that the circle is set. In this study the clearest improvements came from people who started in their fifties and sixties — reconnecting with estranged family, turning acquaintances into regular company. Fifty is not too late for eighty.
e.g. Getting back in touch with old classmates at sixty lifted both mood and medical results across the decade that followed.

### Q: How do I use it today?
Where you are: you're trading health for career, or filing relationships under 'later'.
Ask first: in the last month, how many times did I see someone for no practical reason? If you can't count one, it isn't a 'later' problem.
Where it goes wrong: reading it as needing lots of friends — the data is about quality, not headcount; or using it to force yourself to keep a draining relationship, which is precisely the most damaging category in the data.

### Lines to keep
Your body at eighty is decided by your relationships at fifty.
A marriage held together for the children bills both bodies.
'My circle is already set' is usually a conclusion you reached alone.

========================================================================
## Harvard Study of Adult Development · Relationships need training, like a body
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/harvard-study/social-fitness/
Source: Robert Waldinger's term, social fitness
Tags: Deep read, Harvard Study of Adult Development, Untrained, they decline

Everyone knows a body declines without training. So do relationships. What social fitness actually asks you to do.

### Q: What actually happened?
Waldinger attached a phrase to the study's conclusion: social fitness. Relationships behave like muscle — you don't finish them, and untrained they decline. Very few people in the study fell out with anyone. They moved once, changed jobs once, got busy for a few years, and by the time they looked up the numbers were still in the phone and the people were gone. The action he gives is small: pick one person and get in touch this week, not to arrange anything, just to say how things are.

### The parts · It isn't whether you have them, it's whether it moved recently
Most people judge that they 'have friends' from their contact list and their memory. What does the work is the live part — the people you have actually exchanged something with in the last six months. Counted that way, the number is usually far smaller than assumed.
e.g. Two thousand contacts, fewer than ten spoken to in six months. That second number is the real size.

### The parts · Small moves beat plans
'We should get together more' almost never happens, because it names no day and no person. What works is the smallest step: one message to one person about nothing in particular. The bar is low enough to survive a busy month, and going quiet is what relationships can't survive.
e.g. One person a week is fifty a year. Waiting until things calm down is usually zero.

### The parts · Which gap to fill depends on which one is empty
The study separates relationships by what they do: someone to fall back on, someone to enjoy things with, someone to say the true thing to, someone whose judgement you want. They don't substitute. Find the empty slot first, then decide who.
e.g. A crowd to drink with and nobody to call at 2am isn't a shortage of socialising.

### Q: How do I use it today?
Where you are: you don't think of yourself as unpopular, but when you actually need someone you don't know who to call.
Ask first: who have I contacted in the last six months for no practical reason? Write the names. If you can't reach five, start there.
Where it goes wrong: turning it into a task with a streak — a relationship that becomes a metric is harder to keep; and it doesn't mean reviving everyone. You're training a few lines, not the whole address book.

### Lines to keep
Nobody sets out to lose a friend. They get busy and it goes quiet.
'We should get together' fails because it names no day and no person.
People to drink with and one person to call at 2am are different things.

========================================================================
## Harvard Study of Adult Development · Who can you call at 2am
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/harvard-study/someone-to-count-on/
Source: A measure used throughout the study
Tags: Deep read, Harvard Study of Adult Development, The count doesn't matter, the catch does

The shortest way to measure your relationships. Why this question is so hard to fool.

### Q: What actually happened?
The study has long used one very short question to measure relationships: if you were sick or frightened at two in the morning, who could you call. It beats 'how many friends do you have' because it asks three things at once — whether the person exists, whether you believe they'd pick up, and whether you could bring yourself to dial. Miss any one and the answer is blank. Plenty of socially busy people have no name here; plenty of quiet ones name two or three immediately.

### The parts · Three tests in one question, so it can't be gamed
Someone to call tests supply. Believing they'd answer tests quality. Being able to dial tests you. Other people supply the first two; only you can clear the third — and a lot of people stall there, carrying it alone rather than making the call.
e.g. You can think of the name, and then: 'it's too late to bother them.' That's the third test.

### The parts · No name doesn't mean no one
This answer is found by trying, not by thinking. A relationship you've never asked anything of is one whose strength you don't know. And asking the first time is usually easier than imagined — most people feel trusted rather than imposed upon.
e.g. After the first real ask, the relationship usually gets closer, not more distant.

### The parts · Turn it around: whose name are you
The question works in reverse. Does anyone think of you at two in the morning? Being someone's fallback runs both ways, and being permanently filed as 'lovely, but I wouldn't trouble them' is a shallow relationship. Letting people impose on you is its own kind of reliability.
e.g. Nobody ever asking you for help may not mean you're well-liked. It may mean nobody expects you to say yes.

### Q: How do I use it today?
Where you are: you want to know how solid your relationships actually are, and have no way to measure it.
Ask first: who could I call at 2am? Write the names down. If none come, don't panic — ask the follow-up: is it that there's no one, or that I couldn't make the call?
Where it goes wrong: using it to rank the people around you or tally what you owe; and a blank answer is not a verdict. It measures where you are now, not who you are.

### Lines to keep
If something happened at 2am, who could you call.
No name may not mean no one. It may mean you never asked.
Letting people impose on you is its own kind of reliability.

========================================================================
## Arlie Hochschild · The second shift
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/hochschild/second-shift/
Source: The Second Shift, 1989; time-use surveys of the 1960s–70s
Tags: Deep read, Arlie Hochschild, The shift that starts when work ends

Housework and care have never appeared on a timesheet. Who ends up paying when nobody counts them.

### Q: What actually happened?
In 1989 Hochschild gave the thing a name: the second shift. Women with jobs came home to another one — cooking, cleaning, children, ageing parents, all unpaid and absent from every statistic. Adding paid and unpaid hours from the time-use surveys of the period, she found women worked about 15 hours a week more than men, which over a year is an extra month of 24-hour days. The power of the concept isn't the accusation. It made invisible labour countable.

### The parts · Work that misses the timesheet is paid for by whoever does it
Any work that isn't measured gets treated as something done in passing. It doesn't disappear for going unrecorded; it becomes one person's invisible load, and that person often has no language to complain in, because on paper nothing happened.
e.g. 'You don't work, you're at home' stings because it prices a ten-hour day at zero.

### The parts · List it before you divide it
Most negotiations about chores fail not because nobody will share but because the two people are looking at different lists. Write every task down with the hours it takes each week and the argument moves from 'you don't appreciate me' to a table you can work on.
e.g. Log two weeks: who did what, how long. The gap is usually between what's remembered and what happened.

### The parts · Care time can't be compressed, only moved or dropped
You can stay up late and write a document faster. You cannot feed a child faster or sit with a sick parent faster. Care work is close to rigid in duration, so 'efficiency' barely applies. It can only be taken over by someone else, or not done — and then someone else pays.
e.g. Families hoping better organisation will free up time usually free up sleep.

### Q: How do I use it today?
Where you are: the work at home lands on you, and saying so has changed nothing.
Ask first: are the two of us looking at the same list? If not, spend two weeks writing it all down before discussing who does what.
Where it goes wrong: using the concept as a moral charge, which turns the conversation into a tally of old debts; or the reverse — 'it's hard on everyone' erases the list all over again.

### Lines to keep
About 15 hours more a week. A year of that is an extra month.
The first shift is at work, the second at home. Only one pays.
Labour nobody books gets billed to one person anyway.

========================================================================
## Arlie Hochschild · Emotional labour
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/hochschild/emotional-labor/
Source: The Managed Heart, 1983; fieldwork with flight attendants, waiters and debt collectors
Tags: Deep read, Arlie Hochschild, That smile isn't hers

Some jobs ask you not only to do the work but to feel the right thing. What that requirement costs.

### Q: What actually happened?
In 1983, after fieldwork with flight attendants, waiters and debt collectors, Hochschild named emotional labour: work that requires you to display a prescribed feeling — warmth for the attendant, hardness for the collector. Her central observation was alienation. That smile is not 'her' smile, and over time the worker becomes estranged not only from the expression but from what she actually feels, unable to tell which happiness is her own. She placed it beside physical labour: required feeling is workload, only nobody clocks it.

### The parts · Surface acting and deep acting cost differently
Surface acting is putting the face on while knowing you're putting it on. Deep acting is persuading yourself you really feel it. The first exhausts through tension; the second exhausts because afterwards you can't find yourself again. Both have a bill. They arrive at different times.
e.g. A day on the support line and no words left by evening — that's surface. Years in and feeling hollow is the other bill.

### The parts · Only once you count it as work can you schedule recovery
As long as feelings are treated as your own private business, no rest can ever be arranged for them. Admit that it's workload and you start scheduling recovery the way you would after physical work, instead of expecting the feeling to bounce back on its own.
e.g. Twenty minutes of not speaking to anyone after a run of clients is maintenance, not slacking.

### The parts · The cost rises with the distance from what you feel
The further the required feeling sits from the real one, the more expensive it is. Being asked for warmth while you're grieving costs far more than being asked for calm while you're calm. The most damaging roles aren't the busiest — they're the ones that most often require the opposite of what you feel.
e.g. Straight off an abusive complaint call and into the next one in the same bright voice. That second is the most expensive.

### Q: How do I use it today?
Where you are: you got little done today and can't face saying a word this evening.
Ask first: how much of today was spent holding a required feeling? Was any of that counted as part of my workload?
Where it goes wrong: using it as licence to drop basic courtesy and professionalism; or the reverse — using 'it's the job' to push yourself into deep acting until you can't tell what's real. That's precisely the cost she documented.

### Lines to keep
That smile is not 'her' smile.
In time you're estranged not just from the face but from what you feel.
Required feeling is workload. Nobody clocks it.

========================================================================
## Huineng · There was never a thing there
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/huineng/originally-not-a-thing/
Source: Platform Sutra, chapter one
Tags: Deep read, Huineng, Subtraction is harder than addition

Two verses. Everyone admired one; the other went to an illiterate kitchen worker. What separates them.

### Q: What actually happened?
The fifth patriarch asked his students for a verse to decide his successor. Shenxiu, the head monk and everyone's expected heir, wrote on the corridor wall at night: the body is a bodhi tree, the mind a bright mirror's stand; polish it constantly, let no dust settle. It is an entirely correct account of practice — wipe daily, keep the dust off. Huineng, illiterate and pounding rice out the back, had his written beside it: there was never a tree, nor any stand; there was never a thing there, so where would dust settle? He doesn't dispute the polishing. He asks where the mirror came from.

### The parts · Shenxiu's verse isn't wrong. It's heavy
'Polish it constantly' is executable, checkable and almost impossible to get wrong. The trouble is it can never be finished: as long as you assume a mirror that gets dirty, wiping has no end. A great deal of effort is stuck in that correct, infinite loop.
e.g. Managing anxiety with more lists, more reviews, more reminders. The stack grows and the anxiety doesn't move — each addition is one more thing to maintain.

### The parts · Ask who installed the premise
Huineng's move pushes the question back a layer: don't optimise the solution, audit the setup. 'There was never a thing there' means the object you keep wiping may be one you erected yourself. Remove the premise and the whole discipline goes with its anxiety.
e.g. 'Everyone has to be satisfied with me' makes every conversation exhausting. Ask who set it. Usually you did, and it can be unset.

### The parts · Subtraction is hard because it has no progress bar
Adding a method gives you something to do immediately. Removing a premise gives you nothing to do at all. The second pays far better and shows no progress along the way, so most people keep wiping.
e.g. Cutting half the meetings beats adding a collaboration tool. The first produces nothing to report, so almost nobody does it.

### Q: How do I use it today?
Where you are: something you're managing carefully has never once got lighter.
Ask first: does this need constant managing because it's inherently like that, or because I set a premise?
Where it goes wrong: reading subtraction as giving up; optimising only at the level of solutions and never inspecting the setup.

### Lines to keep
There was never a thing there, so where would dust settle?
Not the wind moving, not the flag moving. Your mind is moving.
The object you keep wiping may be one you put there.

========================================================================
## Huineng · The practice is here, not elsewhere
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/huineng/in-the-world/
Source: Platform Sutra, chapters two and three
Tags: Deep read, Huineng, There is no better place to start

People wait for a quiet enough setting to begin. Why Huineng said that setting doesn't exist.

### Q: What actually happened?
Asked whether a layperson could practise at home, Huineng was flat about it: the teaching is in the world, and awakening is not apart from the world; to seek it outside the world is to hunt for a rabbit's horns — the thing simply isn't there. He pulled the whole practice back into daily life: if the mind is level, what need of precepts; if conduct is straight, what need of meditation. He lived it too — after receiving the transmission he spent fifteen years among a band of hunters, taking the days as they came.

### The parts · There is no better place to begin
Waiting for a quieter environment, an emptier calendar, a riper moment is itself a form of avoidance. To seek it outside the world is to hunt a rabbit's horns — the fully-prepared place doesn't exist, because the conditions never all arrive.
e.g. 'I'll start exercising when this project ends.' There is another project after it. People who start, start while busy.

### The parts · The ordinary thing in front of you is the training ground
Huineng breaks practice down into specific actions inside specific relationships: how you treat your parents, how you treat those above and below, what you do when treated unfairly. None of it needs separate time. It already occupies all of your time; it just wasn't counted as practice.
e.g. The hardest call of the day and the message you least want to answer are that day's entire curriculum.

### The parts · Complete form isn't the same as the thing done right
'What need of precepts, what need of meditation' doesn't abolish either. It warns that form serves substance. When someone's forms are immaculate, that is often exactly when the substance has gone wrong — the form became the substitute.
e.g. The team with the most beautiful process documentation is sometimes the worst at executing. The document felt like the work.

### Q: How do I use it today?
Where you are: you're waiting for a better moment to begin something that matters.
Ask first: if that moment never arrives, what is the smallest step available today?
Where it goes wrong: turning preparation into procrastination; substituting completeness of form for completion of substance.

### Lines to keep
The teaching is in the world. Awakening is not apart from it.
To seek it outside the world is to hunt for a rabbit's horns.
If the mind is level, what need of precepts.

========================================================================
## John Ratey · Exercise is for the brain
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/john-ratey/exercise-for-the-brain/
Source: Spark; the Naperville school programme
Tags: Deep read, John Ratey, You can feel the return the same day

Filing exercise under the gym leaves the cheapest medicine unused. What it's actually changing.

### Q: What actually happened?
A high school in Naperville, outside Chicago, ran an experiment: move PE to first period, and stop measuring who runs fastest — students only had to hold their own high heart-rate zone. That cohort went on to score far above their peers in international maths and science assessments. Ratey uses it to show the link isn't mystical: exercise prompts the brain to release proteins that support neuron growth and connection, which he calls fertiliser for the brain. Exercise doesn't only shape the body. It shapes the brain.

### The parts · Change the motive from your shape to today's state
Aim at your body and the return arrives months later, carried entirely by willpower. Aim at attention and mood and you can feel the return within hours. The second is real, and easier to sustain, because the feedback is fast.
e.g. Attention gone by mid-afternoon: twenty minutes of brisk walking usually beats another coffee, and borrows nothing.

### The parts · Intensity matters more than duration
Naperville had each student hold their own high heart-rate zone rather than race each other. That's good news for ordinary people: you don't need long sessions, you need the heart rate to actually have gone up. Fifteen real minutes beats an hour of strolling.
e.g. With no time, do fifteen minutes that leaves you out of breath rather than an hour of turning up at the gym.

### The parts · Put the hard thing after the exercise
If the window after exercise is when new connections form most readily, then schedule accordingly: the hardest learning or thinking goes after. Moving PE to first period was exactly this logic.
e.g. Before attacking a difficult document, move for twenty minutes. It saves time overall.

### Q: How do I use it today?
Where you are: your head won't turn over and you're forcing it.
Ask first: when did I last actually raise my heart rate? Is twenty minutes of moving a better trade than another hour of grinding?
Where it goes wrong: treating exercise as a cure-all and using it to replace the sleep you need and the problem you should be handling.

### Lines to keep
Exercise doesn't only shape the body. It shapes the brain.
The growth factors physical activity releases are fertiliser for the brain.
Schedule the hardest learning for after the exercise.

========================================================================
## John Ratey · When anxious, move before you think
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/john-ratey/move-before-you-think/
Source: Spark, the chapters on anxiety and stress
Tags: Deep read, John Ratey, Start with the physiology

The more you think, the worse it gets, and knowing that doesn't stop it. Why this is the moment to go outside.

### Q: What actually happened?
Ratey points out how physical anxiety is: the body has already gone on standby and the hormones are circulating, and talking yourself down at the cognitive level barely reaches it. Exercise works because it acts on that system directly — burning off the standby hormones and giving the brain the signal that you already ran and the danger has passed. That explains a common experience: after a walk the thing is less frightening, and nothing about it has changed. So his advice is blunt: when the feeling is jammed, handle the physiology first, the thinking second.

### The parts · Bring the arousal down before you reason
Reasoning at high arousal is extremely inefficient, with yourself or with anyone else. The order should be: get the body down — walk, breathe, leave the room — then return to the content. It's also why reasoning mid-argument doesn't work.
e.g. Chest tight and the same thought circling: go outside for twenty minutes. Come back to the same thing and it weighs differently.

### The parts · Rumination has to be interrupted, not resolved
The twentieth pass over the same thought produces no new information, only a deeper groove. You don't get out of that loop by continuing to think. It needs an external action to break it, and exercise is the most reliable — it occupies attention and burns the hormones at once.
e.g. Catching yourself chewing the same sentence again is the signal to interrupt, not the signal to keep going.

### The parts · Don't let it replace the problem
Exercise lowers the intensity of anxiety. It doesn't resolve what caused it. What you buy is a state in which you can think properly, not an escape. The thing is still there when you get back — you can just see it more clearly.
e.g. Running daily to hold down a fear about a decision. However far you run, the decision is still waiting.

### Q: How do I use it today?
Where you are: something has gone round your head many times and each pass makes it worse.
Ask first: am I thinking or ruminating? Move for twenty minutes, then come back to the same thing.
Where it goes wrong: using exercise to avoid, so that once you've moved you never deal with the thing at all.

### Lines to keep
Anxiety is heavily physical. Talking yourself down barely reaches it.
Exercise gives the brain the signal that the danger has passed.
The twentieth pass over a thought produces no new information.

========================================================================
## Carl Jung · You can't run the afternoon on the morning's programme
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/jung/afternoon-of-life/
Source: Jung, The Stages of Life, 1930–31
Tags: Deep read, Carl Jung, Not wrong. Expired

Something feels wrong around forty. Is it a fault? Jung said it's the hour.

### Q: What actually happened?
Jung compared a life to a day. In the morning the task points outward — a career, a family, a place in the world — and the standards come from outside and genuinely work. His observation was that many people stall in midlife not because their capacity declined but because they are still running the afternoon on the morning's programme. His line is severe: what was great in the morning will be little at evening. Not that the programme was wrong. It expired.

### The parts · Stalling is usually the hour, not a malfunction
Someone in their late thirties doing well and suddenly unable to summon anything looks first for a defect: tiredness, wrong industry. Jung offers another reading — the morning's task is largely done, the afternoon's hasn't been picked up, and the gap between them is the feeling.
e.g. Having everything you were meant to want and feeling emptier is harder to explain to anyone than having nothing.

### The parts · The morning's fix fails twice as hard in the afternoon
Stuck in the morning, the answer is push harder and ask for more. Use that again in the afternoon and it only packs the empty place fuller. Plenty of people add in midlife — bigger house, higher title — and find the feeling entirely unchanged.
e.g. The promotion made it emptier, which says the thing being added was never on the ledger.

### The parts · The afternoon's task points inward, not outward
Jung says the direction reverses: from acquiring to sorting, from proving outward to picking back up the parts of yourself that never got used. The judge changes too — the morning is scored by others, the afternoon only by you.
e.g. Picking up the thing you put down at twenty, mostly not in order to achieve anything with it.

### Q: How do I use it today?
Where you are: you're in your thirties or forties, doing reasonably well, and increasingly unable to summon anything, without being able to say what's wrong.
Ask first: is the effort I'm making still answering the morning's question? If that one is largely answered, adding more won't work.
Where it goes wrong: using it as a reason to abandon a career — Jung is describing a shift of weight, not walking off; and don't read every bout of tiredness as a turn in your life. Sometimes you're tired.

### Lines to keep
What was great in the morning will be little at evening.
Adding more in the afternoon only packs the empty place fuller.
The direction reverses: from proving outward to picking yourself back up.

========================================================================
## Carl Jung · What you push down comes back
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/jung/the-shadow/
Source: Jung on the shadow and projection
Tags: Deep read, Carl Jung, It jumps out of other people

The kind of person you can't stand — why they can enrage you instantly. Jung said part of you is in there.

### Q: What actually happened?
Jung called the part of yourself you deny and push down the shadow. To become an acceptable person, everyone suppresses something: ambition, laziness, temper, wanting to be seen. Those things don't disappear. They move somewhere you can't see, and then jump out of other people. So the kind of person you least tolerate usually carries the very thing you won't own. The harder it was pushed down, the faster you're enraged.

### The parts · Disproportionate dislike is a signal
Not liking someone is ordinary. But if the reaction is out of proportion — the mention of them irritates you, you have to comment even when it doesn't concern you — it is probably not only about them. Ordinary dislike doesn't consume this much.
e.g. People who loathe attention-seekers are usually the ones who most want to be seen.

### The parts · Suppressed things don't vanish, they reroute
Jung's framing is conservation-like: what isn't acknowledged finds another exit. It can become fault-finding in others, a sudden loss of control, or a physical complaint. Acknowledging it is the least-effort option available.
e.g. The person who never gets angry, when they finally do, frightens everyone including themselves.

### The parts · Owning it isn't acting on it
Admitting you'd also like to slack off, be praised, have the ambition, is not the same as slacking or grabbing. Jung means putting it back into consciousness where it can be managed — what's hidden can't be, what's on the table can.
e.g. People who can say 'I want that position too' are less likely to do something ugly to get it.

### Q: How do I use it today?
Where you are: there's a type of person you can't think about without anger, and you know your reaction is too big.
Ask first: which exact quality am I reacting to? Write it down, then ask whether I have it and never let it out.
Where it goes wrong: using it to excuse every dislike — some people should be disliked; and owning something isn't permission to do it. You own it in order to manage it.

### Lines to keep
When the dislike is out of proportion, it isn't only about them.
What you push down doesn't vanish. It changes exit.
You own it in order to manage it, not to act on it.

========================================================================
## Carl Jung · Wear the mask long enough and it grows in
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/jung/the-persona/
Source: Jung on the persona
Tags: Deep read, Carl Jung, Necessary, but it has to come off

What happens after years inside a role. Jung says the mask isn't the problem — here's where the problem is.

### Q: What actually happened?
Jung used the word mask for what a person puts on outside: the post, the identity, the version of you others expect. The mask is necessary; without it you can't deal with the world. The danger lies elsewhere — wear it long enough and you take it for yourself. Then every judgement starts from the role, and when the role is removed — retirement, redundancy, children leaving — whoever is left finds they don't know who to be.

### The parts · A mask isn't dishonesty. It's a necessary interface
The voice you use at work, the way you are with clients — masks, and they should exist. Jung isn't asking anyone to take theirs off. He's asking that you can tell them apart: which part the role requires and which part is yours. Telling them apart is what keeps it removable.
e.g. Still using your meeting voice at home means this layer isn't coming off easily any more.

### The parts · The moment the role is taken is the moment you find out
Retirement, redundancy, children leaving are the same event: the mask removed from outside. How badly you panic then measures how much of what you built grew only on the role. The more complete the panic, the less the separating was ever done.
e.g. The hardest part of the first six months of retirement is usually not the empty days. It's not knowing who you now count as.

### The parts · Keep one area the role can't reach
In practice: hold on to something unrelated to your identity — an interest, a set of people who don't know your job title. Its usefulness isn't in how important it is but in not moving when the role does. It's what you're standing on when the role goes.
e.g. A group of friends who know your name and not your title is worth more than anything else here.

### Q: How do I use it today?
Where you are: you've been in one role for years and find that with it off, you don't know who you are.
Ask first: if this identity vanished tomorrow, what would be left? If you can write three things, it hasn't grown in yet.
Where it goes wrong: using it to dismiss professional identity — the mask is a necessity, not a burden; and 'being your real self' doesn't mean never adjusting for the room. That removes the interface too.

### Lines to keep
The mask is necessary. The trouble is taking it for yourself.
What's left when the identity goes can't be seen in advance.
Keep one thing the role can't reach. That's what you stand on.

========================================================================
## Garry Kasparov · After losing to it, he changed the rules
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/kasparov/advanced-chess/
Source: The six-game rematch, New York, May 1997; the first Advanced Chess event, León, 1998
Tags: Deep read, Garry Kasparov, Let people bring machines to the board

When a machine wins at your craft, what's left of it. Why Kasparov invited the computer onto his own board.

### Q: What actually happened?
He beat Deep Blue in Philadelphia in 1996. In the New York rematch of May 1997 it beat him 3.5–2.5, the first time a world champion lost a formal match to a machine. A year later he staged an event in León under new rules: each side brought a computer to the board and could consult it at any time. He called it Advanced Chess. The reasoning was plain — calculation was already lost, so stop competing on who calculates faster.

### The parts · First identify what's no longer worth competing on
The day machines won on depth of calculation, the 'who sees furthest' track closed. Training on a closed track has no exit however hard you train. The first step isn't redoubling effort; it's striking the lost item off your own list of what you're worth.
e.g. Speed of looking things up, of arithmetic, of making a sentence read properly — none of these are things to compete on now.

### The parts · Change the rules, not the effort
He didn't train harder and he didn't switch fields. He changed what the contest permits. When a tool matches an ability, the valuable position moves to how the tool gets used — and somebody has to define that position before it exists.
e.g. Not 'I'll write faster than it' but 'I decide what this piece is and which parts are whose'.

### The parts · Inviting the tool in holds better than keeping it out
A contest that bans tools survives only on enforcement, and collapses the moment enforcement slips. A contest that permits them is measuring something else — something that doesn't expire as tools improve, because it improves alongside them.
e.g. You can ban calculators in an exam. You can't hold that line at work, and the sneaks end up ahead.

### Q: How do I use it today?
Where you are: a core skill in your field has been matched by a tool, and you're still training on the old track.
Ask first: which item in my field is now clearly lost to the tool? Strike it out — what's left that it can't replace?
Where it goes wrong: hearing 'if you can't win, don't train' — he didn't stop playing chess, he stopped competing on calculation; and changing the rules isn't open to everyone. First you have to know the old game well enough to see them.

### Lines to keep
Calculation was already lost, so stop competing on calculation.
The first step isn't more effort. It's striking out what's lost.
A contest that bans tools survives only while enforcement holds.

========================================================================
## Garry Kasparov · The winner wasn't the best human or the best machine
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/kasparov/process-beats-both/
Source: The 2005 PAL/CSS freestyle tournament; Kasparov, Deep Thinking, 2017
Tags: Deep read, Garry Kasparov, It was the pair with the best process

What human plus tool is actually good at. Why two amateurs won a tournament where everyone could use a computer.

### Q: What actually happened?
A freestyle online tournament in 2005 admitted grandmasters and supercomputers, with humans and machines free to team up. The winners were two American amateurs, Steven Cramton and Zackary Stephen, running three ordinary PCs. Their method was to ask all three and apply their own judgement only where the three disagreed. Kasparov later compressed it: a weak human plus a machine plus a good process beats a strong human plus a machine plus a poor one.

### The parts · The value moves from answering well to asking well
Where all three machines return the same answer, adding a person adds nothing. The human value concentrates entirely in the few moves where they disagree — finding the disagreement and judging which side to believe. That is a different job from playing chess.
e.g. Two tools give different conclusions and you can say why you trust one. That's your work.

### The parts · Process makes up for ability; ability can't make up for process
The amateurs won on a stable checking routine. The grandmasters lost by treating the machine as a reference and calling it themselves at the end. The first doesn't depend on how you feel that day; the second does. That is how weaker players beat stronger ones.
e.g. Same tool: one person asks three times and cross-checks, the other asks once and ships it.

### The parts · Don't keep only one tool
With one machine there is no disagreement to look at — you either believe all of it or none of it. Three aren't valuable because the compute adds up. They're valuable because the places they disagree mark exactly where the problem is genuinely hard.
e.g. Ask two different tools the same question. Where the answers fight is where you should be thinking.

### Q: How do I use it today?
Where you are: you already use the tools, and what you get out looks like what everyone else gets out of the same ones.
Ask first: do I have a fixed way of checking? Do I ever put the same question to a second tool?
Where it goes wrong: hearing it as 'just open more tools' — they won on the checking routine, not the count; and don't skip the fundamentals because amateurs won. Recognising a real disagreement takes knowing the subject.

### Lines to keep
Where all three agree, adding a person adds nothing.
The human value sits in the few moves where they disagree.
Process makes up for ability. Ability can't make up for process.

========================================================================
## Garry Kasparov · He spent years arguing the match didn't count
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/kasparov/excuses-cost-years/
Source: His 1997 post-match statement and rematch demand; Deep Thinking, 2017
Tags: Deep read, Garry Kasparov, Conceding is cheaper than appealing

What the first year after being replaced usually looks like. What he did, and what he said twenty years later.

### Q: What actually happened?
After the loss he told the press that IBM had used human intervention mid-match, and demanded a rematch. IBM refused, and dismantled Deep Blue — leaving him without even an opponent to play again. He told that version for years. By the time he wrote Deep Thinking in 2017 he had withdrawn it himself: Deep Blue won, and that is all. The 1997 explanations were what he couldn't accept at the time.

### The parts · Appealing and moving on can't run in parallel
The effort to prove that match didn't count and the effort to work out what to train next come out of the same person in the same stretch of time. The first buys no new skill even when it wins.
e.g. Six months proving the tool was used wrong is six months not spent learning to use it right.

### The parts · The other side isn't waiting for your post-mortem
IBM dismantled the machine, which shows the pattern: whatever replaced you doesn't need your agreement and won't hold a rematch open for you. Hoping to end this by getting the other side to concede is usually a wait with no end.
e.g. A role is cut and it's cut. Nobody comes back to debate whether cutting it was right.

### The parts · Conceding isn't surrendering
The same year he accepted the loss he was staging a tournament under new rules. Accepting a result and giving up the craft are two different things — accepting it first is what freed his hands to change the track. Nobody swallowing their pride changes anything.
e.g. 'The machine is faster at this than me' and 'my field is done with me' are not the same sentence.

### Q: How do I use it today?
Where you are: a tool or a new method has beaten you, and most of your energy is going into explaining that it's unfair or that it isn't actually good.
Ask first: how many times this month have I said it's unfair? In the same month, what new thing did I practise?
Where it goes wrong: hearing it as 'no feelings allowed' — it took him twenty years. The point is not to let the appeal become the only thing you're doing, not to demand you accept it today.

### Lines to keep
Whatever replaced you does not need your agreement.
Proving it didn't count and deciding what to train next cost the same hours.
Accepting the result and giving up the craft are different things.

========================================================================
## Li Ka-shing · Ninety per cent of the time, thinking about failure
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/li-ka-shing/ninety-percent-failure/
Source: Li Ka-shing, interviews, around 2006
Tags: Deep read, Li Ka-shing, Think about losing before winning

The richest man in Hong Kong describes his own split of attention, and it is not what you'd expect.

### Q: What actually happened?
In interviews Li Ka-shing has been blunt about it: ninety per cent of my time I spend considering failure. His image is a mechanical watch — one gear slightly faulty and the whole watch stops, and a company is the same. From his plastic-flowers days the habit was set: before a project starts, work through the ways it can fail. When success comes it needs very little thinking about. Beside it runs his rule on cash: a company can go bankrupt while profitable. Through decades of expansion his gearing stayed low.

### The parts · Rehearsing failure is insurance on the decision
Ninety per cent on failure isn't pessimism, it's a division of labour: failure modes are finite, listable and preventable. Having gone through each and set a gate, you can spend the remaining tenth committing hard. Optimism without that step stakes the company on luck.
e.g. The most valuable page in a project review isn't the market size. It's the list of ways this dies. Fewer than five means nobody has thought yet.

### The parts · Find the gear that stops the whole watch
The watch image is precise about 'one gear'. What sinks a company is often not the main business but some unremarkable connector — a guarantee given, a maturity mismatch, one key person. So rank risks by whether they stop the watch, not by how big the business is.
e.g. Healthy companies die of a guarantee made for someone else, or a licence that wasn't renewed.

### The parts · Cash flow is the floor under every failure case
Every rehearsed way of dying converges on the same place: is there enough in the account to get through. So his answer isn't don't take risks. It's make sure no single failure can cut the cash. Low debt isn't caution. It buys more chances to be wrong.
e.g. Ask of an aggressive plan: can its worst outcome reach the cash artery? If not, be aggressive. If so, slow down even the safe version.

### Q: How do I use it today?
Where you are: a project looks strong and the team is uniformly optimistic.
Ask first: has the list of ways it dies been written? Which gear stops the watch? Does the worst case touch cash?
Where it goes wrong: turning rehearsing failure into only rehearsing failure and never moving; or covering business risks and missing the small gears — guarantees, mismatches.

### Lines to keep
Ninety per cent of my time, I spend considering failure.
One gear with the slightest fault and the watch stops.
A company can go bankrupt while it is profitable.

========================================================================
## Li Ka-shing · Knowing where to stop
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/li-ka-shing/knowing-when-to-stop/
Source: The scroll in his office, widely reported; Cheung Kong's operating principle
Tags: Deep read, Li Ka-shing, The two characters on his office wall

A businessman famous for expansion looks up at a scroll telling him to stop. Stopping and not daring aren't the same.

### Q: What actually happened?
Li Ka-shing's office carries a scroll with two characters usually read as 'know where to stop', from a classical line: know where to stop and then you can be settled. Alongside it is the principle he repeats: never forget stability while growing, never forget growth while stable. In practice that meant selling down in overheated property, and walking away when a bid passed his line — moves others read as missing the market. He hung that scroll during Cheung Kong's most aggressive expansion. The faster you accelerate, the more you need a brake pad in permanent view.

### The parts · Write the stop before you sit down at the table
In practice this means writing the exit condition before every entry: above this price we don't chase, past this amount we don't add, at this date we don't renew. Written while unemotional, it needs no heroism to execute. Recalculating 'is it worth it' in the room is calculating your pride.
e.g. Write your maximum before the auction and give it to a colleague. Every extra pound buys the feeling of not losing, not the asset.

### The parts · What stops is the exposure, not the ambition
This gets misread as contentment with a little. His record says the opposite — decades from plastics to property to ports to telecoms, the ambition never paused. What was capped was the exposure of any single bet. Aggressive on direction, limited per bet: the second is what keeps the first alive.
e.g. Long-term ambition about the field, a hard ceiling on each round. Companies that cross several cycles usually run that combination.

### The parts · Hang the brake pad where you see it daily
Framing those two characters on the office wall is mechanism design. This is the string that goes first when things are going well, so the reminder has to be physically present — hit once a day when you look up. A principle that lives only in the annual speech is gone by the expansion season.
e.g. Print the per-project ceiling and the gearing red line in the header of the decision-meeting template.

### Q: How do I use it today?
Where you are: the market is hot, the team is confident, and you're considering adding more.
Ask first: has the exit condition for this one been written? When — before entering, or just now?
Where it goes wrong: using 'know where to stop' as cover for never acting; or writing the line and then stepping over it because this time is special.

### Lines to keep
Know where to stop, and then you can be settled.
Never forget stability while growing; never forget growth while stable.
What gets capped is the exposure, not the ambition.

========================================================================
## Christina Maslach · Burnout has three parts. Tired is one
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/maslach/three-signs/
Source: Maslach & Jackson, Maslach Burnout Inventory, 1981
Tags: Deep read, Christina Maslach, The other two warn you earlier

Tired and burnt out are not the same thing. The three measures Maslach used to separate them.

### Q: What actually happened?
In 1981 Maslach built an inventory that split burnout into three components: emotional exhaustion (drained in a way sleep doesn't repair), depersonalisation (you start handling people as items, and can't summon interest in any of them), and a fall in personal accomplishment (nothing you do feels like it matters). Only the first overlaps with being tired. So somebody can look like they're working normally and still be delivering, while the other two have been running for months.

### The parts · Detachment warns earlier than exhaustion, and gets misread
Rest fixes tired. It does not fix detachment. Detachment looks like having nothing for colleagues, customers or family, and speech going formulaic. Others read it as someone turning cold; the person reads it as their personality changing. It's the second measure lighting up.
e.g. Your own voice on the phone sounds unfamiliar to you, like reading from a script.

### The parts · 'I'm useless' isn't modesty, it's a reading
The third component is accomplishment collapsing: the same work finished, and where there used to be a little satisfaction there is now nothing. It gets treated as an attitude problem. On the inventory it is as measurable as the other two.
e.g. The project landed and you felt nothing, only wanted it over. That is not being low-key.

### The parts · They don't arrive together, so don't wait for the set
For most people detachment comes first, then exhaustion, and accomplishment collapses last. By the time all three are present, recovery takes far longer than it would have when one appeared. One of the three is enough to take seriously.
e.g. 'I can still handle it' usually means using the one that hasn't shown up to deny the one that has.

### Q: How do I use it today?
Where you are: you suspect you're burnt out and keep telling yourself it's just tiredness.
Ask first: which of the three do I have — drained, nothing left for people, no satisfaction on finishing? Only the first is tiredness. Either of the other two is a different thing.
Where it goes wrong: using it to diagnose yourself and stopping there — it's for locating the problem, not labelling yourself; and don't use it to judge whether someone else is slacking.

### Lines to keep
Sleep fixes tired. It does not fix detachment.
Still working normally and still delivering proves nothing about the other two.
'I can still handle it' denies what's here using what isn't.

========================================================================
## Christina Maslach · Fix the job, not the person
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/maslach/fix-the-job/
Source: Maslach & Leiter, The Truth About Burnout, 1997
Tags: Deep read, Christina Maslach, Teaching people to relax repairs the wrong thing

What to do about burnout. The mainstream answer may have the whole thing backwards, and she says why.

### Q: What actually happened?
The moment burnout was named, the market's fix became teaching people to relax: mindfulness, time management, resilience training. Maslach has argued against that direction for decades. Her claim is blunt: burnout is a problem of the work environment, not of individual resilience. Spending the effort on remaking the individual asks the person absorbing the damage to repair the thing causing it — and carries a second message along with it: if you can't take this, you aren't strong enough.

### The parts · Putting the responsibility in the wrong place makes it worse
Tell someone the problem is their attitude and they add a layer of self-blame, then stay in the same environment. The two together are much harder to climb out of than the exhaustion was on its own.
e.g. The company runs a mindfulness course and doesn't touch the rota. Everyone comes back to the same schedule.

### The parts · Personal fixes aren't useless, they're second
Maslach never said sleep and exercise don't work. She said the order matters: see what in the working conditions can change, then talk about personal regulation. Reverse the order and personal regulation stops being support and starts being cover.
e.g. Cut the two hours of daily meetings first. Then discuss how to unwind. Not the other way round.

### The parts · For an individual, this means check the environment first
You may not be able to change the company, but you can do the accounting: is it too much work, or no say, or work that runs against what you care about? Each diagnosis points at a completely different move — what to negotiate, what to leave, what to refuse.
e.g. You think you need a holiday; the audit says what's crushing you is needing sign-off for everything.

### Q: How do I use it today?
Where you are: you're close to done, and everyone advises you to adjust your mindset and rest more.
Ask first: if I took a month off, would I come back to the same arrangement? If yes, the problem isn't your mindset.
Where it goes wrong: using it to deny everything an individual can do — she gives an order, not an exemption; and don't let it replace medical help. Burnout and depression aren't the same thing, and if you can't tell, see a doctor.

### Lines to keep
Asking the person absorbing the damage to repair its cause is backwards.
A mindfulness course and an unchanged rota send everyone back to the same schedule.
If a month off returns you to the same arrangement, it isn't your mindset.

========================================================================
## Christina Maslach · Six ways to be mismatched
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/maslach/six-mismatches/
Source: Maslach & Leiter's six areas of worklife
Tags: Deep read, Christina Maslach, Workload is only the first

Same hours, and one person breaks while another doesn't. The six places she found the mismatch.

### Q: What actually happened?
Maslach and Leiter split the sources of burnout into six areas — the places where a person and a job fail to match: workload, control, reward, community, fairness and values. Most people watch only the first. In her data the later ones are often more lethal, particularly having no say (control) and doing work that runs against what you believe (values). At identical hours, people matched on all six rarely break; people short two or three break quickly.

### The parts · Little work with no control hurts more than lots with control
Control is the second area and the most underrated. Few tasks, each needing sign-off and liable to be overturned at any moment, costs far more than a heavy load you get to arrange yourself. This matches what the stress research found independently.
e.g. Three things a day, each waiting on three people to nod, is more tiring than ten you decide yourself.

### The parts · A values mismatch is the slowest and the deepest
The sixth area is doing work that runs against what you care about. It doesn't strike the same day; it hollows out the meaning gradually — the longer you do it the emptier it gets, and the less you can say why. Fix the other five and this one still takes you down.
e.g. Having to say things you don't believe every day. No salary fills that particular hole.

### The parts · Score them separately or you can't tell what to move
'Work is exhausting' implies no action at all. Score the six one by one and the answer usually gets specific: what you need to fight for is decision rights, or what you need to raise is fairness, or what you need is different work.
e.g. You think you need less volume; the audit says what's missing is any say in it.

### Q: How do I use it today?
Where you are: you can't say what is draining you, only that you can't keep this up.
Ask first: workload, control, reward, community, fairness, values — which of the six am I clearly mismatched on? One sentence each.
Where it goes wrong: using it to prove quitting is the only option — several of the six are negotiable; and don't fail all six and then do nothing. Move the worst one.

### Lines to keep
Little work needing sign-off costs more than lots you decide yourself.
A values mismatch doesn't strike today. It hollows the meaning out slowly.
'Work is exhausting' implies no action at all.

========================================================================
## Maria Montessori · Change the environment before the behaviour
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/montessori/prepared-environment/
Source: The Casa dei Bambini, Rome, 1907
Tags: Deep read, Maria Montessori, Out of reach is what looks like defiance

Children considered unmanageable changed when the room changed. What was it that actually changed?

### Q: What actually happened?
In a poor district of Rome, Montessori did something then considered absurd: child-sized furniture, tools a child could work alone, children choosing their own activity, adults stepping in only when needed. Three- to six-year-olds thought unmanageable began repeating an activity for tens of minutes and tidying up afterwards. She called the state normalisation, and drew the foundation of the whole method: a child's work isn't taught into them; it happens in a prepared environment.

### The parts · Check whether the environment matches
A cup out of reach, a tool only an adult can operate — these manufacture dependence and frustration. Change the environment so the child can finish alone and the behaviour problem often disappears. It holds for adults too: plenty of self-discipline problems are environment problems.
e.g. The child keeps knocking the cup over. A small jug they can grip beats saying 'careful' a hundred times.

### The parts · Concentration grows, it isn't demanded
She saw children concentrate for a long time on self-chosen work and lose focus quickly on assigned tasks. So the route to concentration is offering attractive choices and not interrupting — and the most common interruption is an adult's well-meant attention.
e.g. The child is absorbed in the blocks. Don't praise and don't correct. Praise interrupts, and moves the motive from the work to your reaction.

### The parts · The adult steps back into observer
This method asks more of the adult than the child: hold back from directing, from doing it for them, from prompting early. Montessori required teachers to learn observation first — see where the child is stuck and what they need, rather than pushing a plan along.
e.g. When the tower won't stand, don't reach in. Watch for thirty seconds. Most of the time they try another way.

### Q: How do I use it today?
Where you are: your child repeatedly can't do something and saying it again hasn't helped.
Ask first: at their height, with their grip, with these tools — is it actually possible? Which single thing in the environment could change?
Where it goes wrong: turning 'change the environment' into removing all difficulty, which leaves nothing to practise on.

### Lines to keep
A child's work isn't taught in. It happens in a prepared room.
Education is not what the teacher said. It's what the child did.
What the adult most needs to learn is to observe and wait.

========================================================================
## Maria Montessori · Help me to do it myself
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/montessori/help-me-do-it-myself/
Source: The Secret of Childhood
Tags: Deep read, Maria Montessori, Doing it for them saves your time

Doing it for them takes two minutes. What those two minutes bought, and what they cost.

### Q: What actually happened?
Montessori compressed the whole method into a child's request: help me to do it myself. That draws the boundary of help — the goal is that they can finish alone, not that the task finishes sooner. What an adult saves by taking over is their own time; what is spent is that one chance to learn. She also described sensitive periods: stages when a child absorbs a particular capacity with almost no effort. Hit the window and it is nearly free. Miss it and the same thing costs several times as much.

### The parts · Lower the difficulty to just within reach
The right intervention is neither taking over nor leaving them to it. It's adjusting the difficulty: break the task to a step they can do now and leave that step to them. It's the same thing deliberate practice calls the edge of the comfort zone, happening at three.
e.g. They spill the water every time. Give them a small container to practise the feel, rather than pouring it yourself from now on.

### The parts · Sensitive periods: wrong timing doubles the work
At two, a child is intensely sensitive to order, and habits of putting things away form easily. Try to establish the same rule at seven and the difficulty is completely different. Reading which period they're in beats working from an age chart.
e.g. Suddenly everything must go back in its exact place. That's not stubbornness. It's the window.

### The parts · Slow is a cost and an investment
Letting a child do it will be slower and messier. Accepting that cost requires a longer time horizon: the ten extra minutes today buys years of not having to be involved. When the arithmetic doesn't get done, adults take over indefinitely.
e.g. Dressing them yourself on a rushed morning is fine. If every morning is rushed, the arithmetic never happened.

### Q: How do I use it today?
Where you are: they're slow and doing it badly and you can't stop yourself taking over.
Ask first: am I taking over so they learn, or so this ends sooner? Could I just drop the difficulty one notch?
Where it goes wrong: turning 'let them do it' into no help at all. Repeated failure makes a child give up outright.

### Lines to keep
Help me to do it myself.
Every unnecessary help is an obstacle to development.
Ten extra minutes today buys years of not being involved.

========================================================================
## Charlie Munger · Invert, always invert
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/munger/invert/
Source: Harvard Law commencement, 1986
Tags: Deep read, Charlie Munger, Study the ways it dies first

He was asked how to have a good life and answered the other question instead. The swap is the whole method.

### Q: What actually happened?
Invited to address a graduating class, he announced he would explain how to guarantee a miserable life, and then worked through it: be unreliable, learn only from your own experience, go down when you take your first reverse, be consumed by envy and resentment. If you knew where you were going to die, he liked to say, you would simply never go there. The talk is the method demonstrated on itself, and it is more usable than any list of virtues he could have read out instead.

### The parts · One list is short and the other isn't
There are countless ways a thing can go well and a small number of ways it reliably goes wrong. The inverted question is simply a smaller problem, and a smaller problem is one you can actually finish.
e.g. Nobody in the room could say what would make the product work. Everyone could name the three things that would kill it, and two were already true.

### The parts · Failure modes are checkable; success stories aren't
You can go and look at whether the runway is short, whether one customer is half the revenue, whether the one person who understands the system is leaving. 'Is this a great idea' has no such test.
e.g. The post-mortem was written before the launch, and two of its causes were fixed in the week it was written.

### The parts · It does not tell you what to do
Avoiding every failure mode leaves you alive, not successful. Inversion clears the ground; something still has to be built on it. Used alone it produces people who are very good at not losing and have not won anything.
e.g. Three years of avoiding every avoidable mistake, and nothing shipped that anyone remembers.

### Q: How do I use it today?
Where you are: about to commit to a plan you believe in.
Ask first: spend twenty minutes writing only the ways this fails, then check how many are already true today.
Where it goes wrong: stopping there — a list of avoided deaths is not a direction, and people who only invert end up very safe and very still.

### Lines to keep
Invert, always invert.
If you knew where you were going to die, you would never go there.
Inversion clears the ground. It does not build anything on it.

========================================================================
## Charlie Munger · One hammer is not enough
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/munger/latticework/
Source: USC Business School, 1994
Tags: Deep read, Charlie Munger, The danger is the skill, not the ignorance

What he warned about was not ignorance. It was being very well trained in exactly one thing.

### Q: What actually happened?
At USC in 1994 he laid out the method of his life: you have to carry a number of models in your head and hang experience on that latticework. He put the count at eighty or ninety, drawn from mathematics, psychology, physics, biology and engineering. The warning attached to it is the line everyone knows: to a man with only a hammer, every problem looks like a nail — and the man with the hammer is not the ignorant one, he is the well-trained one.

### The parts · The deeper the training, the better hidden the distortion
The hammer problem is not incompetence. It is that your discipline arrives with a viewfinder: the finance person sees a cost problem, the growth person a funnel problem. Each account is coherent, because any problem does have that face — and the coherence is what stops the search.
e.g. Churn was diagnosed as a pricing problem for three quarters by the only people who were asked, who all came from pricing.

### The parts · Problems do not arrive by department
A pricing decision is economics and psychology and, because the competitor reacts, something close to biology. The latticework means laying several models over the same situation and seeing which one explains the most, rather than which one you already own.
e.g. The retention question turned out to be a queueing problem, and nobody in the room had ever been handed that model.

### The parts · Load the models before you need them
A model you go and look up during the decision arrives too late to shape it. The models have to be in the head and automatic. There is no shortcut: take the two or three hardest ideas from each field and keep them.
e.g. He read about critical mass years before the network product, which is why the question came up in week one instead of year two.

### Q: How do I use it today?
Where you are: diagnosing a problem inside your own speciality.
Ask first: how would someone from a completely different field describe this? If you cannot produce a second account, you have one model, not a diagnosis.
Where it goes wrong: collecting models as trivia — the test is whether one of them changed a decision.

### Lines to keep
To a man with only a hammer, every problem looks like a nail.
The hammer man is not the ignorant one. He is the trained one.
A model you look up during the decision arrives too late to shape it.

========================================================================
## Esther Perel · Security and desire want opposite things
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/perel/security-and-desire/
Source: Esther Perel, Mating in Captivity, 2006
Tags: Deep read, Esther Perel, Which is why the better it gets, the flatter

The steadier life gets, the less you feel, and most people assume they changed. Perel says the structure did it.

### Q: What actually happened?
Perel has done couples therapy for over thirty years, and the sentence she hears most is: everything is fine, we just don't feel anything. Her explanation blames nobody. Intimacy wants closeness, familiarity and predictability; desire wants distance, the unknown, the thing not yet fully held. Both are real needs and they point in opposite directions. So the more settled a relationship, the more easily the second gets squeezed out — not love going wrong, but one thing perfected until it crowds out the other.

### The parts · It isn't love fading. Two needs are crowding each other
Read as love fading, the only available moves are blaming yourself or blaming them. Read as two needs crowding, the move is clear: not repairing the love, but making room again for the one that got squeezed out.
e.g. Ten years together, everything fine, nothing there. Not one word of that sentence says the love went wrong.

### The parts · Familiar to the point of no unknown leaves nothing to miss
Desire needs a little opacity. When their schedule, thoughts and reactions are all inside your predictions, missing them has nowhere to land. So the problem often isn't too little communication — it's everything being accounted for.
e.g. Both schedules known to the hour is often the first bit of air a long relationship loses.

### The parts · Room comes from separateness, not more closeness
The instinct is more time together, more talking. Perel's prescription often runs the other way: each go and do something the other isn't part of, become two people again, then come back. Distance isn't the enemy of love. It's the fuel of desire.
e.g. A few days apart and then meeting: that touch of strangeness is useful, not a warning sign.

### Q: How do I use it today?
Where you are: no fights, no crisis, and no feeling, and you can't say what's wrong.
Ask first: when did we last each do something separately and come back with something to say? If you can't recall, start there.
Where it goes wrong: using it to justify neglect — making room isn't withdrawing; and it doesn't mean falling in love again from scratch. This is about clearing space, not applying more force.

### Lines to keep
Intimacy wants closeness. Desire wants distance. Both are real.
'Everything's fine, we feel nothing' says nothing about love failing.
When everything is accounted for, missing them has nowhere to land.

========================================================================
## Esther Perel · Feeling nothing isn't the same as something being wrong
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/perel/not-a-problem-to-solve/
Source: Perel's distinction in couples work
Tags: Deep read, Esther Perel, First tell a wound from an emptiness

'We can't go on like this' can sit on top of two completely different things. Tell them apart before you act.

### Q: What actually happened?
Perel warns about a common misdiagnosis: treating flatness as if it were rupture. Rupture has a wound — contempt, betrayal, sustained attack — and that needs mending. Flatness has no wound; it is simply empty, and emptiness needs filling, not mending. The two moves point in opposite directions: mending a wound means stopping first, apologising first, making it safe first; filling an emptiness means going outward and adding something new. Get it wrong and it worsens — apologising when you should be adding, booking trips when you should be apologising.

### The parts · Check for a wound before choosing a move
The test is concrete: in the last three months, has there been contempt, dragging up old grievances, belittling in front of others? If yes, that's the wound and it comes first. If none of it, this is emptiness, and the treatment is entirely different.
e.g. Never fighting and growing quieter, versus every argument reopening old accounts. Two different illnesses.

### The parts · For emptiness, more communication makes it worse
Repeatedly sitting down to discuss the relationship when it's empty talks away the last of the ease. What it needs is experiencing something new together, not analysing why there's no feeling — the analysis itself turns the relationship into a task.
e.g. The weekly scheduled 'let's talk about us' often turns life into a status report.

### The parts · Only after telling them apart is 'should we leave' answerable
People decide about leaving while the two states are mixed together, so the answer keeps swinging. See first whether it's a wound or an emptiness, then ask — the answers under those two premises were never meant to match.
e.g. Asking whether to break up over and over usually means the previous step hasn't been done.

### Q: How do I use it today?
Where you are: you don't fight and you aren't close, and you're weighing mending against leaving.
Ask first: in the last three months, any contempt, old grievances, belittling in front of others? Yes — that's a wound, handle it first. No — it's emptiness, and wound treatment is the wrong tool.
Where it goes wrong: using 'it's just flat' to cover a real wound; and equally, reading ordinary dullness as proof the relationship has broken.

### Lines to keep
A wound is mended, an emptiness is filled. Opposite directions.
Talking it through while empty talks away the last of the ease.
Ask whether to leave before telling them apart and the answer swings.

========================================================================
## Esther Perel · It isn't how often. It's not being there
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/perel/quality-not-frequency/
Source: Perel on presence in long relationships
Tags: Deep read, Esther Perel, Present in the room, absent in attention

You live in the same place. So why does it feel like long distance? What she says to count instead.

### Q: What actually happened?
Most people count time: how many evenings a week, how many meals together. Perel says that's the wrong ledger — what decides the quality isn't how long you're together but how many moments both people were actually there. Two people on the same sofa on separate phones have spent a whole evening together and zero minutes present. She asks clients something very concrete: when did you last look at each other and talk with no screen interrupting?

### The parts · Count 'together' and 'present' separately
They're different ledgers: together is duration, present is attention. The first stacks up easily; the second can be zero for a whole week. What makes someone feel loved is the second, and it has almost nothing to do with the first.
e.g. A whole weekend together, and afterwards you can't say what they were thinking about for either day.

### The parts · Presence can be practised, and it's cheap
It doesn't need large blocks of time: fifteen minutes a day, person facing person, phones face down, is enough to change how it feels. The difficulty isn't the duration, it's not glancing away — one break and that stretch is over.
e.g. Fifteen minutes before sleep with no phone does more than an expensive holiday.

### The parts · Long enough absent and it reads as not caring
They don't know what your head is busy with. All they can read is where your attention goes, and from that, where they rank. So sustained distraction doesn't communicate 'I'm busy'. It communicates 'you're not important'.
e.g. Listening while answering messages: they remember none of what you said, only that you were looking elsewhere.

### Q: How do I use it today?
Where you are: you're together every day and drifting further apart.
Ask first: when did I last look at them and talk without touching my phone? If you can't name the day, start there before discussing the relationship.
Where it goes wrong: turning it into a new metric to hold over them; and it doesn't mean being present every waking moment. Fifteen real minutes a day, not permanent standby.

### Lines to keep
Together counts duration. Present counts attention.
Same sofa, separate phones: zero minutes present.
Sustained distraction says 'you're not important', not 'I'm busy'.

========================================================================
## Pu Songling · Forty years of sitting the exam
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/pu-songling/forty-years-of-failing/
Source: Chronology of Pu Songling; his preface to Strange Tales
Tags: Deep read, Pu Songling, Never passing, and never a turning point

There's a kind of failure with no decisive battle in it. How you get through that kind of life.

### Q: What actually happened?
At nineteen Pu Songling sat the entry examinations and came first at county, prefecture and circuit level. He was locally famous. Then he sat the provincial examination for the rest of his life, from his twenties into his sixties, and never once passed, supporting his family as a live-in tutor. At seventy-one he was granted a minor honorary status by seniority. No single year in all of it was decisive — not one big defeat and a restart, but once every three years, each time just short, until he was old.

### The parts · Failure with no turning point is the hardest kind
