Lose a battle and you can review it and change direction. Forty years of being just short offers no single event worth reviewing and no signal about whether to stop. Most advice about handling failure assumes there is a turning point to point at. Here there isn't one.
e.g. Six years of sitting the same qualifying exam, a few marks short every time. That isn't one failed venture.

### The parts · He didn't stop, and he didn't make it everything
Worth noticing: he neither gave up the exam nor staked the whole of his life on it. The tutoring continued, the family was kept, the stories were collected. Running them in parallel means that when the thing that never worked fails again, something else in your hands is working.
e.g. While the main thing refuses to happen, the important part is not letting it become the only thing you do.

### The parts · You may keep more than one ruler
The examination was a ruler handed to him from outside, clear and unambiguous — which is exactly what makes it easy to let it become the only one. He had a second: how many stories this year. The second doesn't make the first easier. It stops there being one reading.
e.g. If a whole year yields only 'failed again', that isn't a year in which nothing happened.

### Q: How do I use it today?
Where you are: something you've worked at for years hasn't happened, and you can't say when it would.
Ask first: this year, apart from the thing that didn't happen, what did move? If you can't name one, fill that gap before deciding whether to continue.
Where it goes wrong: using him to argue that persistence pays — he never passed; or the reverse, that he should have quit. He didn't quit. He just didn't let it be the only thing.

### Lines to keep
No year was decisive. Just short every time, until he was old.
A lost battle can be reviewed. Being just short cannot.
Don't let the thing that never works become the only thing you do.

========================================================================
## Pu Songling · The main thing failed. The side thing didn't
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/pu-songling/the-side-thing/
Source: His preface to Strange Tales, and its posthumous publication
Tags: Deep read, Pu Songling, And he never knew

What he spent his life trying to do never happened. What he did on the side did. Can that be arranged?

### Q: What actually happened?
Pu Songling's real work, as he saw it, was the examination. Strange Tales from a Chinese Studio was a diversion — forty years of writing, circulated in manuscript among friends, and he did not live to see it printed. Of the people who remember him today, essentially none do so for his examination essays. The thing ranked first didn't happen and the thing ranked last did — and he died not knowing it.

### The parts · You don't get to set the ranking
Where a thing sits in your own ordering and what it eventually grows into are unrelated. The first is decided by today's standards; the second takes decades to show. So 'which is the main thing' is a question that, asked at the time, usually gets the wrong answer.
e.g. The thing you push hardest often yields nothing, and the thing done casually is what people remember.

### The parts · But don't therefore do both casually
Strange Tales wasn't written carelessly — forty years, nearly five hundred pieces, revised repeatedly. It was last in his ranking, not last in his investment. A side thing can only grow into something if it gets real investment; it just doesn't get the status.
e.g. The moment 'it's only a side project' reaches the investment, it really does become only a side project.

### The parts · Don't wait until you approve of it to take it seriously
He never considered it his achievement. If you have to wait until you can admit 'this is my real work' before putting the hours in, a great many things simply never grow. The steadier practice is to work seriously and leave the ranking undecided.
e.g. Do it properly for five years and then look back at which one worked, rather than choosing now.

### Q: How do I use it today?
Where you are: your day job is flat and the thing you do in the evenings keeps growing, and you don't know whether to swap them.
Ask first: how much have I actually put into the side thing over three years? Talk about swapping after the investment is there, not before.
Where it goes wrong: using him to justify doing several things half-heartedly — he did two things for forty years; or rushing to promote the side thing. Rankings are only accurate looking back.

### Lines to keep
The thing ranked first failed. The thing ranked last didn't.
It was last in his ranking, not last in his investment.
Wait until you approve of it and many things never grow at all.

========================================================================
## Pu Songling · Collecting stories by the road
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/pu-songling/collecting-at-the-roadside/
Source: The tea-stall account, told by later writers rather than by him
Tags: Deep read, Pu Songling, Using the hours nobody wants

Forty years of a tutor's scattered hours. What he did with them, and how the material accumulated.

### Q: What actually happened?
There is a persistent account that Pu Songling set out tea by the roadside and asked passers-by for strange stories, waiving the price of a bowl for each one, then wrote them up at home. It comes from later writers, not from him, and may not be literal. But it matches a checkable fact: he spent forty years as a live-in tutor in gentry households, with a great deal of scattered time around the teaching, and the nearly five hundred pieces accumulated across exactly those years. He didn't quit the job to write. He wrote on the job.

### The parts · Accumulation needs somewhere fixed for things to land
Scattered hours turn into something not because there are many of them but because there is one fixed place that catches them. A thing overheard, a sentence that occurs to you — all into the same notebook. Without that catch, the same forty years simply disperse.
e.g. Every loose idea into one file beats the same ideas spread across ten places.

### The parts · The material is local. You don't go far for it
His sources were the ordinary talk of villagers in the county he tutored in, not the fruit of travels through famous mountains. What's genuinely scarce isn't remarkable experience. It's the eye that treats what's around you as material — most people have as much of it and aren't collecting.
e.g. The complaints, gossip and small events you hear daily. A year separates the person who writes them down from the one who doesn't.

### The parts · Not quitting is what let it run so long
The tutoring fed him and gave him forty uninterrupted years. Had he staked everything on writing, he probably couldn't have lasted. What kills a side project isn't too little investment. It's gambling your living alongside it and being forced to stop.
e.g. Keeping the job is what let the thing reach its tenth year.

### Q: How do I use it today?
Where you are: you want to do something long-term, you have only scraps of time, and you can't afford to quit.
Ask first: do I have one fixed place that catches whatever comes up? Build that before asking whether there's enough time.
Where it goes wrong: using him to argue against focus — he collected one kind of thing for forty years; or treating 'don't quit' as a reason to delay. What matters is that the catch gets used daily.

### Lines to keep
He didn't quit the job to write. He wrote on the job.
Scattered hours add up because something catches them, not because there are many.
What kills a side project is gambling your living alongside it.

========================================================================
## Rat Park · Swap the cage for a park
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/rat-park/rat-park/
Source: Bruce Alexander et al., the Rat Park experiments, 1978–81
Tags: Deep read, Rat Park, Same rat, different situation

The most famous addiction experiment gave a conclusion against intuition. What happens when you change the cage.

### Q: What actually happened?
The standard 1970s addiction experiment went like this: put one rat alone in an empty cage with two bottles, one water and one laced with morphine. The rat drinks the morphine until it dies. The conclusion looks solid — touch it once and you're finished. Bruce Alexander in Canada asked a different question: what if the cage weren't empty? He built a much larger enclosure with companions, wheels, tunnels and places to hide. Same two bottles, and the rats in the park were far less interested in the morphine.

### The parts · The variable isn't only the bottle. It's the cage
The original design treated the cage as background and the drug as the only variable. Once Alexander made the cage a variable too, the conclusion moved: same rat, same bottle, different situation, very different behaviour. The drug's effect isn't denied. It just isn't the only term.
e.g. The same game, played by a child with nothing on all summer and by a child with things to do, is not the same game.

### The parts · The empty cage is manufacturing the demand
The park rats weren't restrained; they didn't much want it. Alexander later used the word dislocation: pull an individual out of the relationships and position they belong in and they will look for anything that fills the gap. The gap is what's being filled.
e.g. The stretch after moving to a strange city with no friends is when anything becomes easy to get hooked on.

### The parts · This has a boundary, and it has to be stated
Rat Park's replications were not uniformly successful and its interpretation is still argued over. The safe reading is that situation is the chronically underrated term, not the only one. Explaining everything with it delays people who need medical care.
e.g. 'Just change your environment' is true for some people and dangerous advice for others.

### Q: How do I use it today?
Where you are: you want to stop something — the phone, drinking, whatever — and the few attempts you made all ran on holding out.
Ask first: when do I usually do it? Log the last ten times — hour, place, whether you had anything else on. Look at what the gap is.
Where it goes wrong: using it to deny the physiological side of addiction, or to talk someone out of getting treatment. It adds the situation term. It doesn't replace medicine.

### Lines to keep
Same rat, same bottle. Different cage, different behaviour.
They weren't holding out. They didn't much want it.
What's being filled is the gap. The substance was just to hand.

========================================================================
## Rat Park · Back home, most of them simply stopped
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/rat-park/vietnam-veterans/
Source: Lee N. Robins et al., follow-up study of returning Vietnam servicemen, 1974
Tags: Deep read, Rat Park, The hardest natural experiment there is

Is there harder evidence than rats? What the numbers on returning soldiers actually showed.

### Q: What actually happened?
In 1971 the US government discovered an awkward problem: a substantial proportion of American servicemen in Vietnam were addicted to heroin. Everyone braced for a disaster — these men would carry it home into the cities. Robins's team followed them and found the opposite. The overwhelming majority simply stopped once home, with only a small fraction relapsing within a year. Same people, same drug, different place. It is one of the very few natural experiments in addiction research with a sample this size.

### The parts · Its strength is that nobody designed it
Laboratory findings always carry the worry that they were engineered. This one wasn't — nobody sent hundreds of thousands of people to a war and brought them back in order to prove a point. Not being designed is exactly what makes it more persuasive than any experiment.
e.g. The same person, at war and back at home, responds completely differently to the same substance.

### The parts · What changed wasn't the place. It was the whole situation
Coming home swapped out an entire set of conditions: no longer possibly dying at any moment, family instead of fellow soldiers, a job and a schedule, and the substance much harder to get. So changing environment isn't moving house. It's withdrawing the conditions holding it up.
e.g. Only the address changed and the hours, the circle and the pressure are identical. That isn't a change of environment.

### The parts · The fraction who relapsed says something else
Some did continue after returning. That fraction is the reminder: situation explains the bulk, not all of it. Who lands in it has more to do with what home was like and what else was going on than with the drug.
e.g. If the home you return to was already an empty cage, the change of place never actually happened.

### Q: How do I use it today?
Where you are: you're trying to help yourself or a family member stop something, and you've been fighting the substance head-on.
Ask first: what conditions hold this up — hours, place, people, the gap it fills? Removing one at a time beats holding out.
Where it goes wrong: assuming a new city fixes it — what this cohort changed was an entire situation; and don't conclude that willpower doesn't matter. It says willpower shouldn't be the only term.

### Lines to keep
Same people, same substance. Home again, and they stopped.
The weight of this data is that nobody designed it.
Changing environment isn't moving house. It's removing the props.

========================================================================
## Rat Park · Take the cage apart before the willpower
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/rat-park/change-the-cage/
Source: The applied reading of Rat Park and Robins 1974
Tags: Deep read, Rat Park, And where this stops being true

Once you know the situation matters, what exactly do you move? How to take the cage apart one bar at a time.

### Q: What actually happened?
Put the last two pieces together and you get a method that runs against common sense: to stop something, don't fight the thing itself first. Look at what keeps it alive. A habit that lasts usually has a whole set of props — a fixed hour, a fixed place, nothing else to hand, people doing it with you. Withdraw those one at a time and the thing gets harder by itself, whereas fighting it head-on withdraws only your willpower, which is the first thing to run out.

### The parts · Keep the log before you move anything
Log ten in a row: the hour, the place, whether anything else was in your hands, who was there. Most people finish the log and find the trigger isn't craving, it's one recurring empty slot. Finding the slot is worth more than studying how to resist.
e.g. Eight of ten were in bed before sleep. What needs changing is that half hour.

### The parts · Whatever replaces it has to actually work
Removing something leaves a gap, and a gap gets filled back the same way. What worked in Rat Park wasn't the absence of morphine, it was companions, wheels, somewhere to go. So the second step is putting something you genuinely like into that slot, not leaving it bare.
e.g. Replacing the phone with staring at the ceiling rarely holds. Replacing it with something your hands are doing does.

### The parts · When the cage can't be moved, this doesn't apply
The method assumes the cage is movable. Some situations aren't — you can't leave the job, move the family, replace the person. Forcing 'change your environment' there only adds a layer of failure. That's when to find professional help rather than keep pushing on the situation.
e.g. Blaming yourself for not changing an environment you genuinely cannot change is effort in the wrong place.

### Q: How do I use it today?
Where you are: you want to stop something, you've tried, each attempt ran on holding out, and each broke in the same place.
Ask first: for the last ten times — what hour, what place, what state? Find the common factor and move that, not the thing itself.
Where it goes wrong: turning it into a universal explanation that replaces medical help; and don't assume removal is the end. The vacated slot needs filling or it fills itself back.

### Lines to keep
Take apart the props holding it up, not the thing itself.
The trigger is often not craving. It's one recurring empty slot.
The slot you vacate will be filled back the same way.

========================================================================
## Robert Sapolsky · Built for escape, left switched on
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/sapolsky/stress-mismatch/
Source: Why Zebras Don't Get Ulcers
Tags: Deep read, Robert Sapolsky, The problem is that it won't turn off

People and zebras run the same stress system. Why only one of them gets sick from it.

### Q: What actually happened?
The title is the whole argument. Zebras don't get ulcers because their stress response runs for a few minutes. A lion charges: heart rate up, glucose released, immune function paused — and the moment they've escaped, it shuts off. Ours is identical, and we run it against mortgages, managers and an unanswered email. So Sapolsky's verdict is that what makes people ill isn't the stress, it's the response staying on. Its price is suspended repair, digestion and long-term building. Fine briefly. Left on, it diverts the maintenance budget indefinitely.

### The parts · It isn't intensity, it's duration
A week-long sprint doesn't damage anyone. Two years of being permanently on call does. To assess your own state, the question isn't how tired you've been lately. It's when the system was last genuinely switched off.
e.g. One project straight into the next for two years. The body never entered repair mode, which is more dangerous than any single hard week.

### The parts · The cost is charged somewhere you can't see
What gets paused under stress is immunity, digestion and tissue repair, and those debts don't show up the same day. So people misjudge how well they're coping. By the time symptoms appear the account has usually been running a long while.
e.g. Rarely ill through a punishing stretch and flattened the moment the holiday starts. Relaxing didn't weaken you.

### The parts · The specifically human problem is imagination
A zebra starts the response on seeing an actual lion. A person can start the entire thing by thinking about something that might happen. That's the core mechanism of chronic human stress, and why working on the thoughts themselves is a real intervention.
e.g. Rehearsing the worst version of a conversation that hasn't happened produces much the same physiology as having it.

### Q: How do I use it today?
Where you are: tense for a long time, unable to point at what's wrong.
Ask first: when did this system last actually switch off? Has there been any stretch where I wasn't on call?
Where it goes wrong: hearing it as 'stress is all in your head' — real pressure has real physiological consequences. This is about duration, not whether it's genuine.

### Lines to keep
Zebras don't get ulcers because the response runs for minutes.
What makes people ill is the response that won't switch off.
A person can start the whole thing by imagining it.

========================================================================
## Robert Sapolsky · Uncertainty hurts more than intensity
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/sapolsky/predictability/
Source: Thirty years of baboon field research; stress physiology experiments
Tags: Deep read, Robert Sapolsky, Predictability and control

Same pressure, and one person breaks while another doesn't. What the actual variable turns out to be.

### Q: What actually happened?
Sapolsky spent thirty years watching wild baboons in East Africa. Low-ranking animals ran chronically high stress hormones and worse health across the board. But rank wasn't the key thing: at the same low rank, individuals who could anticipate when they'd be harassed, and who had social allies, had markedly better markers. The lab agrees. At the same pressure, predictability and a sense of control cut the damage sharply. That moves the intervention from reducing stress to adding certainty and autonomy — usually far cheaper.

### The parts · Definite bad news beats being left hanging
People and animals adapt to a certain bad. They don't adapt to uncertainty. Which is why delaying an announcement often does more harm than the announcement — for the whole delay, everyone is on call.
e.g. A restructuring where the plan never lands costs more than the plan itself. A firm date saves half of it.

### The parts · Control is a cheap buffer
At identical workload, people who decide their own order and pace show a markedly lower stress response. Adding autonomy doesn't require removing any tasks and cuts the wear substantially.
e.g. Swap 'these five, in this order, today' for 'these five today, you choose the order'. Same load, different experience.

### The parts · Social support is a physiological variable
Baboons with allies, and people with stable relationships, show better markers under equal pressure. This isn't reassurance, it's a measurable difference. Isolation is itself a health risk.
e.g. Keeping one or two colleagues you can be honest with through a brutal project beats an extra hour of sleep.

### Q: How do I use it today?
Where you are: under heavy pressure that isn't going to decrease.
Ask first: is there any way to make what's coming more predictable — a fixed date, a definite answer? Can I take back some say over the order and pace?
Where it goes wrong: turning 'control helps' into needing to control everything, which is a new load of its own.

### Lines to keep
Same pressure. With predictability and control, far less damage.
Low-ranking baboons ran high hormones. The ones with allies didn't.
People adapt to a certain bad. They don't adapt to hanging.

========================================================================
## Su Shi · No wind, no rain, no sun
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/su-shi/no-wind-no-rain/
Source: Dingfengbo, 1082
Tags: Deep read, Su Shi, Switching off the scoring

Everyone else on the road was miserable. He was not. What exactly did he switch off in that moment?

### Q: What actually happened?
In 1082 Su Shi — a Song poet two years into exile, recently released from a prison that nearly killed him — was caught in rain on a country road. The servant with the rain gear had gone ahead. Everyone was wretched; he wasn't. When it stopped he wrote a short poem. It ends by looking back at the road he had just walked: there had been no wind, no rain, and no sun either.

### The parts · Wretched is a verdict, not a fact
Same rain, same road. The difference isn't who got wet. It's who filed the afternoon under 'this is going badly.' Misery needs a scoring system to exist. Switch that off and what's left is water hitting you.
e.g. Same demotion: one person is flattened for three months, another starts something new that week. The facts match. One of them kept looking through the frame.

### The parts · Why not walk slowly
The rain gear is gone. Walking faster gets you marginally less wet and costs you the walk. His line isn't bravado; it's arithmetic: don't spend more of yourself accelerating through the part you can't change.
e.g. It's decided and the result is in. Do the post-mortem once. The replaying changes nothing — it's just running in the rain.

### The parts · The last line is the hard one
'No wind, no rain, no sun' doesn't claim it never rained. It says that from far enough along the road, neither the storm nor the sun is an event. That view is only true afterwards — which is why it's worth borrowing early.
e.g. Stuck on a criticism from one meeting: what share of my memory will this hold in three years? The answer is almost always none.

### Q: How do I use it today?
Where you are: something bad is settled and you keep replaying it.
Ask first: is the pain the thing itself, or the frame I keep putting around it?
Where it goes wrong: reading this as permission not to deal with the problem, or using 'this too shall pass' to skip the thing you should do today.

### Lines to keep
Don't listen to the rain in the leaves. Walk on, and hum.
Looking back at that bleak road — no wind, no rain, no sun.
A bamboo stick and straw sandals beat a horse. Who's afraid?

========================================================================
## Su Shi · Huangzhou, Huizhou, Danzhou
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/su-shi/three-exiles/
Source: Written on My Own Portrait; History of Song
Tags: Deep read, Su Shi, Doing real work where you were sent to rot

Asked at the end of his life to name what he'd accomplished, he named three places he'd been banished to. Why those?

### Q: What actually happened?
A year before he died, Su Shi saw a portrait of himself in a temple and wrote a few lines under it. He had been a Hanlin academician and a minister of rites. He listed none of that. Asked what I accomplished: Huangzhou, Huizhou, Danzhou — his three places of exile, each further from the capital than the last, the third on a tropical island then considered the edge of the world.

### The parts · Treat the exile as a term in office
Sent somewhere with no resources and no future, most people wait it out. He treated each posting as a term: what does this place most lack, and what can I leave behind. Rank sets your authority, not whether you work.
e.g. Moved to a dead-end team you can wait two years for an opening — or ask what the worst thing in this team is and whether you can fix it. One of those leaves you holding something.

### The parts · Leave things somebody can point at
A lake dredged and a causeway built. A society to stop infant drowning. A public clinic. A school on an island that had never produced a scholar. Abstract achievements evaporate when the scoring changes; objects stay.
e.g. Three years in a job — how many things can someone point at and say he did that? If the answer is none, the three years are hard for anyone to credit.

### The parts · He set the measure himself
By the official ledger his career was the titles. By listing three places of banishment he announced that the ruler measuring his life was in his own hand. That isn't consolation. It's taking the scorekeeping back.
e.g. A CV of titles held, or a CV of three things finished — two different accounts of who you think you are.

### Q: How do I use it today?
Where you are: you've been put somewhere with no resources and no prospects.
Ask first: what does this place most lack right now, and what could I leave behind that someone could point at?
Where it goes wrong: treating endurance as a strategy; scoring yourself in titles instead of finished things.

### Lines to keep
Asked what I accomplished: Huangzhou, Huizhou, Danzhou.
While I am here, the water will not take this city.
A heart like burnt-out wood, a body like an unmoored boat.

========================================================================
## Su Shi · I see no bad people
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/su-shi/no-bad-people/
Source: His brother Su Zhe's epitaph for him
Tags: Deep read, Su Shi, Treating a person as a person

A man whose enemies nearly had him executed said he could see no bad people anywhere. This is not naivety.

### Q: What actually happened?
Su Shi was jailed over lines from his own poems and came close to execution. For twenty years afterwards, as two factions traded power, he was demoted again and again — the last time to a tropical island. He opposed the reformers' new laws, then opposed the conservatives when they scrapped every one of them. Neither side could keep him. Late in life he told his brother: I could sit with the Jade Emperor or with a beggar. I see no bad people.

### The parts · Refusing to sort people into sides
Faction logic labels the person first and lets the label decide every interaction after. He judged each measure on its merits and was exiled by both sides for it. Not neutrality — a refusal to use the frame.
e.g. Sort colleagues into 'with me' and 'against me' and you have just guaranteed you will never again receive useful information from the second column.

### The parts · 'Bad person' is an expensive verdict
Once you decide someone is bad, your available moves collapse to guarding and fighting, and both burn enormous amounts of you. Seeing a person with their own situation and interests is what lets you work the actual disagreement.
e.g. Decide he's out to get you and every email needs a paper trail. A year of that costs more than the disagreement ever did.

### The parts · This is not the same as having no judgement
He knew exactly who was working against him, and knew his own mouth was the danger. 'No bad people' describes how he treated people, not how he assessed them. Confuse the two and you become either a pushover or a cynic.
e.g. You can judge that someone can't be trusted with something big and still work with him properly and credit his work. Assessment and conduct are separate.

### Q: How do I use it today?
Where you are: there's history with someone, and now every contact is defensive.
Ask first: if I treat him as a person with his own situation, can this specific disagreement be discussed?
Where it goes wrong: mistaking generosity for having no judgement; letting your assessment of someone dictate how you treat them.

### Lines to keep
I could sit with the Jade Emperor or with a beggar.
I see no bad people.
Like a fly in the food: you spit it out before you rest.

========================================================================
## Su Shi · Clear the ground first
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/su-shi/east-slope/
Source: Letters from Huangzhou; Eight Poems of East Slope
Tags: Deep read, Su Shi, The first thing he did when the salary stopped

Exiled to Huangzhou, his salary essentially gone. The first thing he did was not write poetry.

### Q: What actually happened?
In 1080 Su Shi arrived in Huangzhou holding an empty title, barred from official business, with almost no income and twenty-odd people to feed. What he did first was unglamorous: he petitioned for an abandoned military plot east of town — fifty acres of scrub hillside, which he and his family broke themselves — and planted wheat and rice, dug a well, built a house. 'East Slope' is not a poetic sobriquet. It's the name of the field. The poems came after the ground did.

### The parts · Solve eating before you solve meaning
When income stops, the easiest thing to do is work out what this means about you. His order was the reverse: get this month and next year fed, and put the rest later. Not a refusal to think — thinking done hungry doesn't count anyway.
e.g. Newly out of work, the job is to do the arithmetic and find the next inflow, not to re-found your identity.

### The parts · He also kept a ledger
Arriving in Huangzhou he split what money was left into thirty portions and hung them from a beam, taking one a day and saving the remainder in a tube for guests. The point isn't the amount. It's that 'how long can I last' became a number he could see.
e.g. Savings divided by monthly spend. Write the number of months down and keep it somewhere visible — a fear with a number attached is half the size.

### The parts · What you make gives you a place to stand
The field produced more than grain: it produced a name. He stopped being a demoted official and became the layman of East Slope. When the old position is taken, finishing one concrete thing grows a new one faster than waiting to be recognised again.
e.g. One small complete thing finished while unemployed puts you back on your feet faster than a hundred applications.

### Q: How do I use it today?
Where you are: the income has stopped, or is about to, and you're circling what it means about you.
Ask first: where does this month's and next month's money come from? Write the numbers down, then count the months.
Where it goes wrong: reading this as never think long-term — he wrote his best work on that field; and 'farming' means any concrete thing that produces income now, not manual labour.

### Lines to keep
Meaning arrived at while hungry mostly doesn't count.
When the old place is taken, finish one small thing.
A fear with a number attached is half the size.

========================================================================
## Su Shi · The mud had to go somewhere
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/su-shi/silt-into-a-causeway/
Source: Hangzhou, 1090
Tags: Deep read, Su Shi, Turning the by-product into the thing

Dredging a lake leaves you holding the mud. What he did with it is still there a thousand years later.

### Q: What actually happened?
By 1090 West Lake at Hangzhou was half weed and silt, and Su Shi, posted there as prefect, put twenty thousand men on clearing it. That solved one problem and created another: the spoil had to go somewhere, and carting it out of the city would have cost more than the dredging. He laid it across the water instead, as a causeway with six bridges. A walk that had taken most of a day around the shore became a short crossing. It still carries his name.

### The parts · The waste is only waste until you name a use
Nobody asked him to build a causeway; the job was to clear the lake. The mud became a road because he was willing to ask what else it could be, at the moment everyone else was asking where to dump it.
e.g. The meeting notes nobody reads are the onboarding doc nobody has written.

### The parts · Solve it where the work already is
He did not start a second project. The men, the boats and the spoil were already on the water — the causeway cost the difference between carting mud away and setting it down in a line.
e.g. The cheapest test is the one that rides along with a release you were shipping anyway.

### The parts · The real job came first
The causeway is what people remember, but the case he argued was for the lake: without it the farms lost their water, the canal silted, the brewing tax fell. The road was what the work left over, not the reason for it.
e.g. Keep the tool you built on the way, but don't stop the job to build tools.

### Q: How do I use it today?
Next time a job leaves you with something to get rid of — a half-finished draft, a dataset built for one question, a team freed up by a cancellation — spend ten minutes on what it could be before you spend an hour on where it goes.

### Lines to keep
The spoil from the dredging is the causeway.
Everyone was asking where to dump it. He asked what it could be.
The road was what the work left over, not the reason for it.

========================================================================
## Su Shi · I dare not write
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/su-shi/no-more-writing/
Source: Letters after the Crow Terrace poetry case
Tags: Deep read, Su Shi, Stopping the defence is a decision

After his own words were used to build a case against him, did he keep writing? The question is which kind he stopped.

### Q: What actually happened?
In the Crow Terrace case, Su Shi's poems were read line by line as evidence of slander against the throne. He spent over a hundred days in prison and nearly lost his life. Afterwards, in letter after letter to friends, the same sentence: I dare not write. It wasn't fear — he wrote his most famous work in those same years. What he stopped was a different thing: defending himself, arguing who was right. He kept the two clearly apart.

### The parts · You pay for the defence yourself
Arguing over who was right spends your hours and the other person's patience, and winning returns neither. Worse, it has no end: every reply earns another, unless somebody stops. Stopping isn't conceding. It's capping the cost.
e.g. Answering every objection in the comments until 2am, and waking up to three more.

### The parts · It's an action you can tell you took
'Let it go' can't be executed — there's no way to know you've done it. 'I don't write that kind of thing anymore' can: next time your fingers move, you know what you're doing. A mood can't be kept. An action can.
e.g. Write it and don't send it. Leave it 24 hours. Most of the time you no longer want to.

### The parts · Know which kind stops and which continues
He stopped the defending, not the writing. The distinction matters: putting down the pen entirely is self-punishment and takes the real work with it. Only one kind should stop — the kind whose purpose is to make someone admit you were right.
e.g. Correct the record once. The second time is usually no longer about the record.

### Q: How do I use it today?
Where you are: you're being misread or blamed, you keep explaining, and it keeps getting worse.
Ask first: is the next thing I write meant to make the facts clear, or to get someone to say I was right? If it's the second, that's the sentence to stop at.
Where it goes wrong: hearing this as say nothing — clarify a fact once; and don't stop the real work along with it. He stopped the defence, not the writing.

### Lines to keep
He stopped defending himself. He did not stop writing.
Every reply earns another, unless somebody stops.
'Let it go' can't be done. 'I don't write those' can.

========================================================================
## Sun Tzu · Win first, then fight
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/sun-tzu/win-before-fighting/
Source: Art of War, Form
Tags: Deep read, Sun Tzu, The work happens before the clash

Everyone quotes it as bravado. Read slowly it says the opposite: by the time you are fighting, it is mostly decided.

### Q: What actually happened?
The line is four characters longer in Chinese than in any translation, and it is built as a pair: the victorious army wins first and seeks battle afterwards, the defeated army fights first and looks for the win afterwards. It is not advice about how to fight. It is a claim about when the outcome is set. The book spends its early chapters on measurement — ground, numbers, supply, weather, the character of the commander — because that is where the decision actually happens.

### The parts · Preparation is not the same as planning
A plan is a description of what you intend to do. Preparation is changing the conditions until the intended thing becomes easy. The first can be done at a desk in an afternoon; the second takes months and shows up as very little visible activity.
e.g. The negotiation that went well was decided in the six weeks of getting a second supplier to the point of being usable.

### The parts · If it needs courage, something upstream went wrong
Reaching for nerve is usually the sign that the conditions were not set. Sometimes there is no choice. But treating courage as the plan converts an upstream failure into a personal one, and hides the part that could have been fixed.
e.g. He had to wing the board meeting because the numbers had not been reconciled the week before, and afterwards told himself he was bad under pressure.

### The parts · Not starting is a move
If the conditions are not there, the strongest available action is to not begin yet. This is the hardest part to practise, because waiting looks identical to doing nothing, and only one of them has a reason.
e.g. They held the launch a quarter and shipped into a market that had already heard of them, instead of into silence.

### Q: How do I use it today?
Where you are: something is coming that you are bracing for.
Ask first: what would have to already be true for this to go well? Write the list, and see how much of it is still available to change.
Where it goes wrong: reading it as never act until certain — the book is about setting conditions, not about waiting; and the conditions include a deadline.

### Lines to keep
The victorious army wins first and seeks battle afterwards.
The defeated army fights first and looks for the win afterwards.
If it takes nerve, look at what was left undone upstream.

========================================================================
## Sun Tzu · Know both, and know which is harder
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/sun-tzu/know-both/
Source: Art of War, Attack by Stratagem / Estimates
Tags: Deep read, Sun Tzu, Your own numbers are the flattered ones

Quoted for two thousand years, usually as a case for research. The half everybody skips is the one about yourself.

### Q: What actually happened?
The Estimates chapter is not a maxim, it is a form to fill in: five dimensions and seven comparisons — whose ruler has the way, whose commanders are abler, who has the ground and the season, whose discipline is enforced, whose troops are stronger, whose are better drilled, whose rewards and punishments are clear. Then a coldly practical conclusion: if the count comes out favourable, fight; if it does not, don't. He called it reckoning in the temple — settle it before you decide whether to go at all.

### The parts · Knowing is a filled-in table, not an impression
'I have a rough sense of the competition' is not knowing. The value of a list of comparisons is that it forces out the row you cannot answer, and the row you cannot answer is usually the one that decides it.
e.g. Nobody could say what their support costs per account were. That empty cell was the entire margin difference.

### The parts · Your own side is the harder half
Their information is outside you and can be gone and found. Yours has been through several people who each had a reason to round it kindly. The order in the sentence puts them first; the difficulty runs the other way.
e.g. The competitor's timeline came from their own blog. His own timeline came from a manager reporting to the person who set it.

### The parts · The count has to be allowed to say no
More reckoning wins, less reckoning loses. The point of the exercise is not to find a way to win; it is that it can output 'this one should not be fought'. A process that ends in action whatever it computes is not a decision, it is a ceremony.
e.g. Every quarterly review ended with the same launch date. The review was not deciding anything and everyone knew it.

### Q: How do I use it today?
Where you are: about to commit to something competitive on the strength of a general sense.
Ask first: which rows can you actually fill in, and which is blank? Go and fill the blank one before anything else.
Where it goes wrong: turning it into endless analysis — the count has a deadline, and 'we cannot know' is itself a row.

### Lines to keep
More reckoning wins. Less reckoning loses.
Theirs is outside and findable. Yours has been through people.
A process that ends in action whatever it computes is a ceremony.

========================================================================
## Sun Tzu · The best fight is the one nobody has
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/sun-tzu/win-without-fighting/
Source: Art of War, Attack by Stratagem
Tags: Deep read, Sun Tzu, Winning a hundred times is not the top of the list

A hundred victories sounds like the ceiling. He says it isn't, and the reason is arithmetic rather than modesty.

### Q: What actually happened?
The chapter gives a ranked list that runs against instinct: attack the enemy's plan first, his alliances second, his army third, and his walled cities last. Each step down costs more and returns less. On sieges he is unusually specific — three months to prepare the engines, three more for the ramps, and a commander who loses patience and sends men up the walls like ants, a third of them dead and the city still standing. He calls that the disaster of assault.

### The parts · Winning is also spending
A hundred victories is not the height of skill; subduing the enemy without fighting is. Every win costs people, money, time and trust. The side that won five times can easily be stronger than the side that won a hundred.
e.g. They won the pricing war and came out of it with a team that had shipped nothing new for a year.

### The parts · Plan, then alliances, then force
Attacking the plan means making their approach stop making sense on its own terms. Attacking alliances means removing the support it rests on. Neither requires contact. By the time only fighting is left, the first two were skipped or botched.
e.g. The integration deal with the distributor ended the competitor's route to market without a single price change.

### The parts · The most expensive move is the one you take personally
Assault happens when there is nothing else left, or when someone cannot stand to walk away. He singles out the commander who attacks in anger. Losing a third of your strength to a wall you did not need is a decision made by a mood.
e.g. The lawsuit was about being right. Two years and a quarter of the budget later, it was still about being right.

### Q: How do I use it today?
Where you are: locked into a fight you expect to win.
Ask first: what does winning this cost, and what would have to be true for it not to be necessary at all?
Where it goes wrong: reading it as avoid all conflict — the ranking has fighting on it; it is just not at the top.

### Lines to keep
Winning a hundred battles is not the height of skill.
Every win you take spends people, money, time and trust.
A third of your strength on a wall you did not need.

========================================================================
## Sun Tzu · The flank only works if the front holds
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/sun-tzu/orthodox-and-surprise/
Source: Art of War, Energy
Tags: Deep read, Sun Tzu, A clever move on its own is a donation

Everyone wants the unexpected move. The chapter is mostly about the unglamorous thing it has to stand on.

### Q: What actually happened?
The Energy chapter asks why the same troops behave like a rolling log one day and a scattered crowd the next. His answer is the pairing: engage with the orthodox, win with the extraordinary. The orthodox is the part that meets them head on and holds; the extraordinary is what comes from the side. He insists the two convert into each other endlessly — which means today's surprise, once used, becomes tomorrow's front.

### The parts · Without the front, the flank hits air
The surprise works because the other side is already gripped and cannot turn. Let the front go slack and the clever move lands on nothing, with your best people stranded out in the open.
e.g. The campaign was inventive and the sales team could not answer the second question, so it produced attention and no orders.

### The parts · A surprise used once becomes the expected thing
Any unexpected move, once used and written up, enters the other side's expectations and becomes part of the front. Planning to live for years off one trick is spending a one-time resource as if it were income.
e.g. The referral loop worked brilliantly, was copied within two quarters, and is now the baseline everyone has.

### The parts · Position, not heroics
The chapter ends not on cleverness but on structure: put the rock at the top of a thousand-foot mountain and the force of it coming down is not the rock's. Seek it in the position, and do not demand it of the people.
e.g. Before asking the team to try harder, someone should ask why the same work takes three approvals.

### Q: How do I use it today?
Where you are: pinning your hopes on one inventive move.
Ask first: what is holding the front while that move happens, and is it actually holding?
Where it goes wrong: concluding that only the basics matter — the front alone defends and never wins.

### Lines to keep
Engage with the orthodox, win with the extraordinary.
Used once, the surprise becomes the thing they expect.
Seek it in the position; do not demand it of the people.

========================================================================
## Sun Tzu · Take the shape of what you meet
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/sun-tzu/form-like-water/
Source: Art of War, Weak Points and Strong
Tags: Deep read, Sun Tzu, Avoiding the strong part is the hard half

'Be like water' became a poster. The chapter is stricter than the poster, and most of it is about what not to do.

### Q: What actually happened?
The chapter is about who is setting the terms: bring the enemy to you; do not be brought to him. Strike what he must defend and he has to come. Decline the engagement and he cannot force it. Then the image everybody knows: water has no constant shape, it avoids the heights and runs to the low ground, and an army has no constant form either — it avoids what is solid and strikes what is hollow.

### The parts · Having no fixed shape is the point
What water resembles is not softness, it is the absence of a preset form. Its shape is decided entirely by what it meets. Which makes 'what is our style of competing' a question with a flaw built into it.
e.g. The playbook that won the first market was applied unchanged to the second, where the constraint was regulatory rather than technical.

### The parts · Avoiding the solid part is discipline, not opportunism
The hard half is the avoiding. The places that look most worth taking, most prestigious, most expected of you are usually exactly where they are thickest. Declining them means absorbing internal pressure, which is harder than spotting the gap.
e.g. Everyone wanted the flagship account. The three unglamorous ones nobody was fighting over paid for the year.

### The parts · Who wrote this week's calendar
Initiative is not moving first. It is that the other side has to answer at your tempo. There is a simple test: look at the week you just had and ask whether you scheduled it, or whether their moves did.
e.g. Four of the five priorities were reactions to a competitor's announcement, and nobody had decided that was the plan.

### Q: How do I use it today?
Where you are: reacting to a competitor, or defending the position you are proudest of.
Ask first: where are they actually thin, and what would it cost you internally to walk away from the thick part?
Where it goes wrong: using it to justify having no strategy at all — no fixed shape is not the same as no direction.

### Lines to keep
Bring the enemy to you; do not be brought to him.
Water has no constant shape. That is what it is being praised for.
Did you write this week's calendar, or did their moves?

========================================================================
## Tao Te Ching · Whatever peaks, turns
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/tao-te-ching/reversal/
Source: Tao Te Ching 40
Tags: Deep read, Tao Te Ching, The top is where to start worrying

Usually read as comfort for bad times. It is more useful as an instrument, and it is sharpest when things are going well.

### Q: What actually happened?
Four characters: reversal is the movement of the way. The claim is not that things get better, nor that they get worse. It is that anything carried to its extreme starts producing its opposite. Which means the most dangerous moment is not the trough — it is the peak, because that is where nobody is looking for the turn. In the trough the rule is working for you and nothing needs to be done about it.

### The parts · Read it at the top, not at the bottom
In a bad stretch the line reads as reassurance and asks nothing of you. In a good stretch it asks a question you would rather not answer: which of the things carrying us right now is at full stretch, and what happens when it stops.
e.g. The year revenue doubled is the year nobody asked what share of it came through one partner.

### The parts · Extremes, not durations
It says nothing about how long anything lasts. A thing at moderate stretch can run for decades. What turns is what has been pushed as far as it goes — margin at its thinnest, hours at their longest, patience at its end.
e.g. The team was not tired because two years had passed. It was tired because the last four months had run at the rate of a launch week.

### The parts · The move is to give something back early
If the turn is structural, the cheap version is to stop short of the extreme on purpose: take some off the table, keep the slack, decline the last increment. The expensive version is to have it taken from you at the turn.
e.g. He cut his own hours in the good quarter, which cost output, and was the reason he was still there for the bad one.

### Q: How do I use it today?
Where you are: something is going unusually well and you are being asked to push it further.
Ask first: what is at full stretch right now, and what breaks when it stops?
Where it goes wrong: reading it as fatalism, or as a reason not to grow — it is about not running any single thing to its limit, not about staying small.

### Lines to keep
Reversal is the movement of the way.
The dangerous moment is the peak, because nobody is looking for the turn there.
Stop short of the extreme on purpose, or have it taken at the turn.

========================================================================
## Tao Te Ching · The part you don't do
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/tao-te-ching/wu-wei/
Source: Tao Te Ching 37, 57, 63
Tags: Deep read, Tao Te Ching, A list of moves to leave out

Usually translated as non-action and read as passivity. It is closer to a list of the moves that make things worse.

### Q: What actually happened?
His verdict on governing is cold: the more prohibitions there are, the poorer the people; the more laws are published, the more thieves there are. The alternative he offers is not letting go. It is: I do nothing and they transform themselves, I stay still and they correct themselves, I leave them alone and they prosper. The load-bearing word is themselves. The point is not to stop things happening; it is to stop being the thing that prevents them.

### The parts · Subtracting moves, not making none
In learning you gain daily; in the way you lose daily. Getting good at running something is largely removing the actions that look like management and function as interference. Take out enough and the thing moves on its own.
e.g. Cancelling the weekly status meeting is what finally got the status written down where anyone could read it.

### The parts · There is a mechanism behind more rules, more problems
Every prohibition creates an incentive to route around it, and every correction leaves room for the next deviation. This is not a claim about morality; it is that a control grows the behaviour it was built to stop.
e.g. The expense policy got three pages longer and the number of creatively categorised dinners went up.

### The parts · Act while it is still small
Deal with the difficult while it is easy, the large while it is small. Non-action is not never acting — it is moving the action earlier, when a small one is enough. Wait and you need a large one, and large ones have consequences of their own.
e.g. A ten-minute conversation in March, or a reorganisation in September. It was the same problem.

### Q: How do I use it today?
Where you are: about to add a rule, a process or a meeting to fix something.
Ask first: which existing action is producing this problem, and what happens if you remove it instead?
Where it goes wrong: reading it as never intervene — it argues for intervening earlier and smaller, not less.

### Lines to keep
The more laws are published, the more thieves there are.
Every prohibition creates a reason to route around it.
Deal with the difficult while it is easy.

========================================================================
## Tao Te Ching · Go to the low ground
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/tao-te-ching/water/
Source: Tao Te Ching 8, 66
Tags: Deep read, Tao Te Ching, Not competing is a choice of location

Water has been praised for two thousand years. The text credits it with one specific thing, and it is about position.

### Q: What actually happened?
He gives water two lines, and both are needed. It benefits all things without contending — and it settles in the places people find distasteful. The second is what makes the first possible: not contending is not a posture, it is a choice of site. He is blunter later — the reason the rivers and seas are king of the hundred valleys is that they are good at being below them. Things flow to you because you are lower.

### The parts · Not contending means standing where nobody is
The line is usually read as moral advice and is closer to geometry: if the position you are in is one nobody wants, the act of contending does not arise. It is settled at the siting stage, not in the fight.
e.g. Everyone was building the assistant. He built the boring importer that all of them needed and none of them wanted to own.

### The parts · The places people find distasteful
Low competitive density hides in the work that is dirty, slow, or takes years to show a result. Those positions are empty precisely because they look bad and produce nothing reportable for a long time.
e.g. Nobody wanted the migration. The person who took it ended up the only one who understood how the whole thing worked.

### The parts · Height stops the flow
If you want people, information or resources to come to you, you have to be positioned below them. This is most visible with information: the higher the posture, the less of what is actually happening reaches you.
e.g. Nobody brought him bad news for a year, and he took that as evidence there wasn't any.

### Q: How do I use it today?
Where you are: choosing what to work on, in a space where everyone is going for the same thing.
Ask first: which necessary job is empty because it looks unrewarding, and what would being there let you see?
Where it goes wrong: mistaking it for accepting bad treatment — the low ground is a position, not a status.

### Lines to keep
It benefits all things without contending, and settles where people find distasteful.
The rivers rule the valleys by being below them.
The higher the posture, the less of what is happening reaches you.

========================================================================
## Tao Te Ching · The empty part is the useful part
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/tao-te-ching/usefulness-of-emptiness/
Source: Tao Te Ching 11
Tags: Deep read, Tao Te Ching, What you left out is doing the work

Which part of a wheel is doing the work? The chapter is short enough to be a definition and it underwrites the whole book.

### Q: What actually happened?
Three parallel examples: thirty spokes share one hub, and because of the nothing at its centre the cart is useful; clay is worked into a vessel, and because of the space inside it holds; doors and windows are cut for a room, and the emptiness is what you live in. One conclusion: what is there provides the advantage, what is not there provides the use. The visible part gets the credit. The gap does the job.

### The parts · Slack is not waste
The schedule with every slot filled, the interface with every field used, the plant run at full capacity — all have removed the room that absorbs surprise. One thing goes off plan and there is nowhere for it to go.
e.g. The team with two unbooked afternoons absorbed the outage. The fully booked one moved every deadline by a week.

### The parts · The empty place belongs to nobody
The hole in the hub is not owned by any spoke, and that is exactly why the wheel turns. Organisations need the same thing: capacity that belongs to no department, available for whatever actually turns up.
e.g. The unassigned engineer was the reason the incident was handled the same day instead of entering a queue.

### The parts · Less is what makes it usable
Function is not improved by addition. Everything added spends someone's understanding and someone's maintenance. The hard judgement is never what else could go in; it is what should be left out.
e.g. Removing four of the seven options doubled the number of people who finished the setup.

### Q: How do I use it today?
Where you are: a plan, a schedule or a product that is full.
Ask first: where is the room for the thing you did not predict? If there is none, the plan only works if nothing surprises you.
Where it goes wrong: using it to defend doing less — the point is deliberate space, not low effort.

### Lines to keep
What is there provides the advantage. What is not there provides the use.
The hole in the hub belongs to no spoke, which is why it turns.
The hard judgement is what to leave out.

========================================================================
## Thomas Gordon · The I-message
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/thomas-gordon/i-message/
Source: Parent Effectiveness Training
Tags: Deep read, Thomas Gordon, Say the effect, not the character

The same event, said one way, starts a fight; said another, starts action. Where the structural difference is.

### Q: What actually happened?
Gordon studied under Carl Rogers and turned his teacher's clinical stance into steps ordinary parents could learn. The core tool is the I-message, in three parts: the specific behaviour, its actual effect on me, and how I feel. Use an I-message, not a you-message: say what this does to me, not what kind of person you are. It works because no part of it judges the other person, so there's nothing to defend against, and the effect is a fact they can't argue with. Most people's default is the you-message — you're so careless, you never help — and every one of those defines the person.

### The parts · All three parts, or it doesn't work
Behaviour alone is a statement. Feeling alone is emotion. Only with all three does the other person see why it needs to change. The part most often dropped is the middle one — the actual effect — and that is exactly where the persuasion lives.
e.g. 'Things on the stairs, I can't see them carrying a box and I'll fall, and that worries me.' All three, and it gets moved.

### The parts · The effect has to be real and concrete
If you can't name an actual effect, this may be a preference of yours rather than a problem. That makes the step a filter as well: when you can't fill it in, ask yourself why you're insisting.
e.g. Their room is messy and it affects nobody. No effect to name means it's a difference of taste, not a problem.

### The parts · An I-message isn't a softened accusation
'I feel you're being selfish' wears the word I and is still a you-message. The test is the subject and the content: are you describing your state or what kind of person they are? The first can't be denied; the second guarantees an argument.
e.g. 'I feel fobbed off' still names their motive. 'I'm getting anxious' is your own state.

### Q: How do I use it today?
Where you are: you need to raise something and you've been holding several sentences in.
Ask first: what is the specific behaviour? What is the actual effect on me? What do I feel? Is there a part I can't fill in?
Where it goes wrong: memorising the three parts as a script and reusing it — people hear the template. What matters is that the content is true, not that the sentence is well-formed.

### Lines to keep
Say what this does to me, not what kind of person you are.
No effect you can name may mean a preference, not a problem.
Most people's default is the you-message, and each one defines them.

========================================================================
## Thomas Gordon · Whose problem is this
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/thomas-gordon/problem-ownership/
Source: Parent Effectiveness Training
Tags: Deep read, Thomas Gordon, Different owner, opposite method

Your child is upset, you explain, and each explanation pushes them further away. What to do in that moment.

### Q: What actually happened?
Gordon's second tool is problem ownership: work out whose problem this is before choosing a method. A child upset about a bad grade owns the problem, and the move is listening. A child wrecking the living room so you can't work — that's yours, and the move is an I-message. Getting it backwards is the common error: parents rush to analyse and advise while the child is hurting, which lays their own anxiety on top. He also noted most parents know only two moves, win or lose, when conflict needn't end with either.

### The parts · When it's theirs, listen and don't lecture
This is counterintuitive, because seeing a child upset makes you want to help. But advice at that moment moves them from solving their own problem to handling your opinion. The right action is to say back what they meant and let them go on.
e.g. 'I'm never going back to school.' Answer 'sounds like something bad happened today' — they'll keep talking.

### The parts · The third method isn't a compromise
Splitting the difference leaves both parties unsatisfied. Gordon wants each side's real need named, then a way that meets both — which often exists and nobody asked.
e.g. They want ten o'clock, you want nine. Nine thirty annoys everyone. Ask, and it turns out they want to finish the game: start before nine.

### The parts · Ownership moves, so keep re-judging
The same situation shifts: a teenager staying up is their problem until it affects the whole household's sleep, and then it's shared. Get the ownership wrong and every subsequent move is wrong, so this is judged repeatedly, not once.
e.g. At first you only listen. Once it starts affecting you, switch to an I-message. Reverse the order and neither works.

### Q: How do I use it today?
Where you are: your child or a colleague is upset and you're about to give advice.
Ask first: whose problem is this? Theirs — listen, and only say back what you heard. Mine — use an I-message and name the effect.
Where it goes wrong: using ownership as a way to hand things off. 'That's your problem' pushes the person away by itself.

### Lines to keep
Work out whose problem this is before choosing a method.
Conflict doesn't have to end with somebody winning.
Advice moves them from solving their problem to handling you.

========================================================================
## Lev Vygotsky · The zone of proximal development
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/vygotsky/zpd/
Source: Thought and Language
Tags: Deep read, Lev Vygotsky, Look at the second line

Two people at the same level today may end up far apart. Which measure the difference shows up in.

### Q: What actually happened?
Vygotsky pointed out that ability has two lines: what a person can do alone, and what they can do with help; between them lies the zone of proximal development. His example is two children who stop at the same point solving a problem alone, and then, given a small hint, one goes a long way further and the other doesn't. Identical actual level, completely different zone — and it's the zone that decides what they can learn next. Against the orthodoxy of his day he argued that teaching should run ahead of development, not wait for it.

### The parts · Assess by the response to a hint
Independent performance alone underestimates the difference. What actually predicts is how far someone moves once given a little help — that shows where they can grow next. For managing people and for teaching children this is the same measure.
e.g. Two reports produce about the same today. Give the same pointer: one advances at once, one doesn't. Invest in the first.

### The parts · Pitch it just above where they are
Hard enough to need help, not so hard that help doesn't get it done. Below that is repetition; above it is discouragement. It's the same location that deliberate practice calls the edge of the comfort zone, named differently.
e.g. Teaching equations to a child who has just learned addition is wasted. So is only ever doing addition.

### The parts · First between people, then inside one
He held that higher thinking happens in interaction first and is internalised after — a child is questioned by adults before learning to question themselves. That is why discussing, retelling and teaching someone else beat reading silently.
e.g. Explain the thing you can't grasp to another person. You're borrowing the structure you haven't internalised.

### Q: How do I use it today?
Where you are: teaching someone or teaching yourself, and unsure where to set the difficulty.
Ask first: can they do this alone? Can they do it with one hint? The stretch between is what to practise.
Where it goes wrong: reading 'run ahead of development' as the further ahead the better. Too far ahead only discourages.

### Lines to keep
Between what you can do alone and with help lies the zone.
Teaching should run ahead of development.
Higher thinking happens between people before it happens inside one.

========================================================================
## Lev Vygotsky · Scaffolding: give it, then take it away
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/vygotsky/scaffolding/
Source: The teaching application of Vygotsky's school
Tags: Deep read, Lev Vygotsky, Left up, it becomes dependence

How much help is the right amount? The test is whether it comes down.

### Q: What actually happened?
Scaffolding is this school's metaphor for help: you put it up so someone can reach higher, and once they've reached, it comes down. Help that stays becomes dependence and leaves the person at the level where they're being held — which is how many patient teachers and parents end up producing students who can't work alone. So every intervention should carry the question of when it will no longer be needed. Whether a piece of help was good isn't judged by whether the task got done. It's judged by whether less support is needed next time.

### The parts · Help should decrease by design
First time, demonstrate one step and have them do the next. Second time, prompt only the opening. Third time, nothing. The decrease is designed, not spontaneous — unless you actively withdraw, help gets waited for.
e.g. Demonstrate the whole solution every time and the child waits for the demonstration and never starts.

### The parts · The test is less support needed next time
Whether help worked isn't whether this problem came out right; it's how many prompts the next one takes. That test transfers directly to managing people and stops you mistaking doing it for them for teaching.
e.g. They finished under your guidance, and the next similar task needs exactly as much guidance. That wasn't teaching.

### The parts · Taking it down too early is also wrong
Scaffolding fails in two directions: left up it creates dependence; removed too early it discourages and pushes someone back into not trying. The pace is set by their response, not by your patience.
e.g. Struggling, give one more line. Making progress, say nothing. The test is their progress, not your discomfort.

### Q: How do I use it today?
Where you are: you're teaching someone and unsure how much to give.
Ask first: when does this help come down? Does the next round need less support?
Where it goes wrong: using 'it has to come down' as a reason to stop helping altogether. It comes down once they can reach.

### Lines to keep
Scaffolding goes up in order to come down.
Whether help worked shows in how much they need next time.
Help that stays leaves people at the level where they're held.

========================================================================
## Wang Yangming · Knowing and doing are one thing
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/wang-yangming/unity-of-knowing-and-doing/
Source: Instructions for Practical Living, part one
Tags: Deep read, Wang Yangming, Not done means not known

'I understand it, I just can't do it.' Wang Yangming argued that the sentence itself is the error.

### Q: What actually happened?
A student objected: plenty of people know they should honour their parents and don't, so knowing and doing must be two things. Wang Yangming's reply closes the road. There has never been anyone who knew and did not act. To know and not act is simply not to know. He adds the test: to say a man knows filial duty, he must already have practised it, not merely be able to use the word. As with pain — to know it is to have hurt.

### The parts · 'I understand but can't do it' is a self-issued exemption
Split knowing from doing and you have carved out a permanently safe position: my understanding is fine, my execution is a little short. 'To know and not act is simply not to know' deletes that position. There is no middle state.
e.g. 'I know I should start earlier, I just procrastinate.' By his test that person hasn't grasped the cost. He has heard about it.

### The parts · Knowing is signed off in the doing
How do you tell whether you actually understand something? Not by whether you can explain it, but by whether you used it in the moment it was needed. Explaining well is one ability. Using it is another, and the first doesn't contain the second.
e.g. You can recite every framework in the negotiation book and still negotiate on old habit. It stopped at the telling.

### The parts · The thought starting is already the act
He puts the start of action extremely early: where a thought arises, the act has already begun. Not when the movement happens — at the instant of the thought. That moves the ground of the work from behaviour back to intention, which means there is no such thing as 'only thinking about it'.
e.g. The first time 'I can fudge this one' occurs to you and you don't cut it off, it has already started.

### Q: How do I use it today?
Where you are: something you keep telling yourself you should do, and have never done.
Ask first: if I can't say when I last did it, on what grounds do I say I know it?
Where it goes wrong: treating 'I've understood it' as a milestone; or policing only behaviour and leaving the thought completely unguarded.

### Lines to keep
There has never been anyone who knew and did not act.
To know and not act is simply not to know.
Where a thought arises, the act has already begun.

========================================================================
## Wang Yangming · You are polished by events
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/wang-yangming/polish-on-things/
Source: Instructions for Practical Living, part three
Tags: Deep read, Wang Yangming, Sitting still trains nothing

Someone said he felt perfectly steady sitting quietly and fell apart the moment anything happened. Why that steadiness doesn't count.

### Q: What actually happened?
A student complained that in quiet meditation things felt clear, and the moment something happened it was different. Wang Yangming's answer: that's because you only cultivate stillness and never do the work of mastering yourself. A person must be polished by events to stand firm. He was his own evidence. After his awakening in exile he didn't return to the cushion; he went on to put down four rebellions in succession, all of it done in the middle of events.

### The parts · Steadiness in a quiet room is fake
With nothing interrupting, everybody is steady. Composure can only be measured while you're being cut off, misread, or pushed against a deadline. A state trained in a silent room scatters the moment something happens because it was never tested.
e.g. The plan made on Sunday is clear and firm. Three urgent messages on Monday and it's gone. The plan was fine. It was never tested.

### The parts · Events are the only training ground
Being polished by events means treating every piece of trouble as the equipment, not as the thing preventing practice. Cultivation and getting things done aren't two activities competing for time. The first can only happen inside the second.
e.g. 'I'll sort myself out once this busy stretch is over', so it never gets sorted. The busyness is the material.

### The parts · Mastering yourself is a specific action
Cultivating stillness without mastering yourself, he said, is a cat watching an empty hole. Mastery isn't a vague resolution to be better. It's holding down one specific impulse at one specific moment: not interrupting when you want to, hearing it out before defending yourself.
e.g. The three seconds after being corrected in public are the only real practice you get all day.

### Q: How do I use it today?
Where you are: you think clearly when things are calm and lose shape the moment you're in the room.
Ask first: when was I last genuinely thrown? What did I do in that moment?
Where it goes wrong: scheduling self-cultivation as a separate project needing a quiet environment; treating interruptions as what breaks the practice rather than as the practice.

### Lines to keep
A person must be polished by events to stand firm.
Cultivating stillness without self-mastery is a cat watching an empty hole.
Steady in stillness, steady in motion — one is not the other.

========================================================================
## Wang Yangming · Act on what you already know
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/wang-yangming/innate-knowing/
Source: Instructions for Practical Living, part two
Tags: Deep read, Wang Yangming, The answer is in your first reaction

Most of what we call being unable to decide is being unwilling to admit. Why he said the judgement is already there.

### Q: What actually happened?
Late in life Wang Yangming compressed everything into three characters usually rendered as 'extending innate knowing'. The knowing is the judgement every person already has: that bit of innate knowing in you is your own standard. The moment an intention stirs, he said, right is right and wrong is wrong, and it cannot be fooled. Don't cheat it, act on it, and that is the whole of it. So the difficulty was never knowing right from wrong. It is admitting the one you already know.

### The parts · The first reaction has usually already answered
Before you have begun finding reasons, the judgement in that instant is generally accurate. The weighing that follows is mostly not a search for the answer. It's a search for an acceptable substitute for the answer you have.
e.g. You see the figures are wrong and know in one second it goes back. The next half hour of 'no time', 'close enough' isn't analysis. It's negotiation.

### The parts · The hard part is not cheating it
Three things cover the knowing: not wanting the hassle, not wanting to look bad, not wanting to offend. Extending it isn't improving your judgement. It's moving those three screens aside so the judgement that's already there can reach an action.
e.g. You know this call is yours to make and hand it to someone else, because 'it lands better from him'.

### The parts · Sages fill the street
If everyone has it, the gap between people in judgement is smaller than we imagine — the gap is in willingness to act on it. That sounds egalitarian and is actually severe: you can no longer plead that you lack the insight.
e.g. The most reliable person on a team is rarely the cleverest. It's the one who does it knowing it's a hassle.

### Q: How do I use it today?
Where you are: you've been turning something over for a long time without deciding, and there has been a direction in you the whole while.
Ask first: what was my judgement in the first second? Are these later reasons testing it, or replacing it?
Where it goes wrong: mistaking unwillingness for lack of clarity and gathering more information; using 'I need to think more' to postpone an answer you have.

### Lines to keep
That bit of innate knowing in you is your own standard.
Everyone has a sage inside. Most bury him by not trusting him.
The difficulty was never knowing. It is admitting.

========================================================================
## Wang Yangming · The bandits inside
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/wang-yangming/bandits-in-the-heart/
Source: Letter to Yang Shide and Xue Shangqian
Tags: Deep read, Wang Yangming, The hardest battle is the interior one

He never lost a campaign. Why he said all of those were the easy ones.

### Q: What actually happened?
In 1518, while suppressing bandits in Jiangxi, Wang Yangming wrote to two students: to break the bandits in the hills is easy; to break the bandits in the heart is hard. He had just put down, with very few troops, an insurgency entrenched for decades — the thing everyone else considered impossible — and he called it easy.
