Bandits in the hills have a form: position, numbers, supply lines, all discoverable. The ones inside have none. They aren't out there. They are the one doing the judging.

### The parts · Problems with a shape are always the easier ones
A problem you can list is already half solved. What really holds a person is the stuff with no name: resentment, fear of being thought less of, a grudge against one particular person. None of it enters any list, and all of it quietly rewrites every decision.
e.g. The meeting lists resourcing, scheduling, dependencies. The real cause may be a bad exchange between two leads three months ago.

### The parts · The interior bandit disguises itself as reasoning
It never arrives looking like emotion. Resentment says 'there's still an opportunity in this direction'. Fear of embarrassment says 'switching now is too expensive'. So you catch it by auditing arguments, not by inspecting feelings — check whether the reason always points at the same conclusion.
e.g. You oppose the same person's proposals every time, and the reason is different every time. The reasons aren't what's operating.

### The parts · Break your own first, then talk about anyone else's
He wrote that letter while commanding troops and governing a province. He didn't file the interior work under things to do once the fighting stopped; he treated it as the inside of the same job. Campaigning outward and mastering yourself draw on one supply of energy.
e.g. A manager who audits every external account and never his own preferences ends up with an organisation shaped like them, and can't see it.

### Q: How do I use it today?
Where you are: something won't move, and you have the full list of external causes.
Ask first: the reasons are different each time — is the conclusion the same each time?
Where it goes wrong: scheduling the interior work for after the job is finished; admitting only the causes that can be written into a list.

### Lines to keep
Breaking the bandits in the hills is easy. The ones inside aren't.
When this mind does not move, you can move with the moment.
The reasons change and the conclusion doesn't. That tells you something.

========================================================================
## Norbert Wiener · He wrote to the union first
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/wiener/wrote-to-the-union/
Source: Wiener's 1949 letter to Walter Reuther of the UAW; The Human Use of Human Beings, 1950
Tags: Deep read, Norbert Wiener, Before automation landed

Is there a move to make before a technology reaches you? What the man who built it did first.

### Q: What actually happened?
Cybernetics was published in 1948, and Wiener was the person who put machine control into the world. The next year he did something nobody was doing: he wrote to Walter Reuther, head of the United Auto Workers, saying automation would displace assembly-line workers on a large scale, that he was unwilling for this to happen with no preparation, and that the union should get involved early. In 1950 he turned the same worry into a book.

### The parts · The people who see it coming usually aren't hit yet
The year Wiener wrote, automation wasn't deployed and nobody had lost a job. Precisely because it hadn't landed, there was time to arrange something. Once it lands you only get to react; there is no room left to prepare.
e.g. The stretch while you still have work and haven't been cut is the only window you get to plan in.

### The parts · Find people in the same position before you find answers
He didn't start by writing a survival guide for workers. He went to the people who were already organised. One person carrying this kind of shock has almost no leverage; tens of thousands do. Making contact comes before working it out.
e.g. Finding people in your field already dealing with it beats sitting alone devising a strategy.

### The parts · The people pushing it and the people hit by it aren't two groups
He was both the inventor and the person raising the alarm, and in him those didn't conflict. The tool you use every day — the better you get with it, the sooner you can see which tasks it will take. Those are exactly the ones to prepare for.
e.g. The work you're saving yourself with it is work somebody else still eats from.

### Q: How do I use it today?
Where you are: something is spreading through your field, it hasn't reached your income yet, and you plan to wait and see.
Ask first: which task of mine can it already do? Who in my field have I actually talked to about it?
Where it goes wrong: reading it as a call to oppose things early — he went to the union to move the preparation forward, not to block automation; and this isn't personal heroism. His first move was to find people already organised.

### Lines to keep
Once it lands you only get to react. There is no room to plan.
Finding people in the same position comes before working it out.
The work you save with it is work somebody else eats from.

========================================================================
## Norbert Wiener · What a machine can do, and what to give it
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/wiener/human-use/
Source: The Human Use of Human Beings, 1950
Tags: Deep read, Norbert Wiener, Two separate questions

Which work belongs to a tool and which doesn't. Why Wiener said capability doesn't settle it.

### Q: What actually happened?
Through The Human Use of Human Beings, Wiener keeps returning to one point: what a machine is capable of and what people are for are two independent questions. Whether a machine can do a task is technical. What is left of the person once you hand it over is a different question, and the answer isn't automatically good. What worried him wasn't machines getting stronger. It was people being arranged to do the machine's kind of work: repetitive, judgement-free, instruction-following.

### The parts · 'It can' does not imply 'it should'
Tool capability and division of labour are separate layers. Hand over everything it can do and what's left is often the scraps it can't do and you learn nothing from. What should go is the repetition, not the judgement.
e.g. Letting it draft is fine. Letting it decide what the piece is arguing hands over the wrong half.

### The parts · The fear is people used as machines
Wiener's worry ran the other way round. He wasn't afraid machines would be like people; he was afraid people would be arranged like machines — executing, not judging, not knowing why. Those roles go first, because they were already designed in a machine's shape.
e.g. A job that works a ticket queue and never asks why is in the first batch automation takes.

### The parts · Keep the part where you decide
Once the repetition is handed over, what has to remain is the stretch that needs a call made. Otherwise you gave away repetition and kept repetition. Judgement doesn't get cheaper as the tools improve. It gets dearer.
e.g. The tool gives you three options. Which one and why is the step you can't also hand over.

### Q: How do I use it today?
Where you are: you're shifting work onto a tool and can't say which part should go and which shouldn't.
Ask first: am I handing over the repetition or the judgement? After it's gone, does anything left on my desk require a decision?
Where it goes wrong: using it as grounds for distrusting tools and doing everything yourself — he objected to handing over the judgement, not the repetition; and it isn't a list of things machines may not touch. He's describing a division of labour.

### Lines to keep
What a machine can do and what people are for are separate questions.
He feared people being arranged like machines, not machines resembling people.
Hand over the repetition. Not the judgement.

========================================================================
## Norbert Wiener · Control is a loop, not an order
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/wiener/feedback-not-command/
Source: Cybernetics, 1948
Tags: Deep read, Norbert Wiener, Seeing the result beats issuing instructions

Why the thing you carefully explained still comes back wrong. How Wiener defined control instead.

### Q: What actually happened?
Cybernetics defines control not as issuing an instruction but as using the actual result to correct the next move — the feedback loop. Wiener's example is reaching for a cup: the eyes keep reporting the gap between hand and cup, and the hand corrects as it travels. Cut that report and the movement immediately goes off, however well it was aimed to begin with. Machines and living things, he said, obey the same thing here.

### The parts · An instruction with no report back isn't control
However clearly you explained it, without a channel carrying the actual result back you hold an intention, not control. Things come back wrong not because people don't listen but because the loop is cut and nobody can tell how far off it has drifted.
e.g. Brief it and wait for delivery, never seeing the thing in between, and what arrives will not be what you pictured.

### The parts · The report has to arrive while it can still be changed
Feedback later than the correctable window is worthless. The value of a loop isn't whether it exists but how often it reports — weekly and daily differ by an order of magnitude in how much drift can still be pulled back.
e.g. Finding out at month end that the month went wrong means the month is already spent.

### The parts · Practising alone runs on the same rule
Stuck on a skill is usually not a shortage of practice. It's the absence of any mechanism reporting the result back: you finish and don't know whether it was good or where it went wrong. More hours won't fix that. A report channel will.
e.g. Months of practice and no progress: first check whether anything tells you which move was wrong.

### Q: How do I use it today?
Where you are: what you asked for keeps coming back different, or you've practised something for months with no progress.
Ask first: how often does the actual result come back to me? Inside that interval, how much is still changeable?
Where it goes wrong: reading it as watch more closely — he means shorten the reporting cycle, not raise the intervention rate. They aren't the same, and the second usually crushes the loop itself.

### Lines to keep
Control isn't issuing an order. It's correcting from the result.
It came back wrong because the loop was cut, not because nobody listened.
Feedback later than the correctable window is no feedback.

========================================================================
## Zhuangzi · The use of being useless
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/zhuangzi/use-of-uselessness/
Source: Zhuangzi, In the World of Men; The Mountain Tree
Tags: Deep read, Zhuangzi, What nobody requisitions lives longest

Making yourself useful is instinct. What being useful costs you at the same time.

### Q: What actually happened?
A master carpenter passes an oak so vast it could shade thousands of oxen, and doesn't look twice. Asked why, he says: it's useless timber — boats from it sink, coffins rot, tools break. Good for nothing, and so it has lived this long. That night the tree comes to him in a dream: the fruit trees get torn apart the moment the fruit ripens; their ability is what harms them. I have sought uselessness a long time, and only now have it. Then Zhuangzi turns it on people: everyone knows the use of the useful; nobody knows the use of the useless.

### The parts · Useful is a qualification to be requisitioned
Once a person is judged unusually good at something, that something arrives without end. It looks like being valued. It is being fixed in one position and spent there — the ability itself becomes the source of the load.
e.g. Whoever is best at firefighting gets all the fires. Three years on, they're the least replaceable and the least improved person on the team.

### The parts · Useless is the room you keep for yourself
The useless tree survived by not appearing on anyone's list. People need a portion of time and ability that isn't counted as output — it produces nothing immediately, and it is the only part nobody else gets to schedule.
e.g. Put half a day a week in the calendar and hold it. Everyone will call it a luxury, and it decides whether you can do anything else a year from now.

### The parts · Don't exhaust yourself in a single position
Zhuangzi isn't against being useful. He's against being useful as the only way of existing. Used to the limit means completely defined, and the moment that use isn't wanted the person expires with it.
e.g. A team that only knows one line of business fails entirely when the cycle ends. Not for lack of effort. They were too competent.

### Q: How do I use it today?
Where you are: you're the one on the team who can carry anything, and you're busier every month.
Ask first: the thing I'm best at — what position is it fixing me in?
Where it goes wrong: treating being needed as safety; converting all of your hours into output you can report.

### Lines to keep
Good for nothing, and so it has lived this long.
Everyone knows the use of the useful. Nobody knows the use of the useless.
The cinnamon is edible, so it is cut down.

========================================================================
## Zhuangzi · The cook and the ox
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/zhuangzi/ox-carving/
Source: Zhuangzi, The Secret of Caring for Life
Tags: Deep read, Zhuangzi, Go along the gaps

One cook replaces his blade monthly, another hasn't in nineteen years. Where exactly the difference sits.

### Q: What actually happened?
Cook Ding carves an ox for Lord Wenhui and the movement looks like dancing. Asked how his technique got so good, he says what he cares about isn't technique. At first he saw a whole ox; after three years he no longer saw a whole ox; now he meets it with the spirit rather than looking with the eye. A good cook changes his blade yearly, because he cuts. An ordinary one monthly, because he hacks. His has done thousands of oxen in nineteen years and the edge is as if newly whetted — because he has been travelling in the gaps between the joints.

### The parts · The blade stays sharp because it never meets the hard part
The edge has no thickness and the joints have space; something thin entering something wide moves easily. Struggle isn't a shortage of force. It's the wrong place to put the blade. Every hard collision is a positioning problem.
e.g. A push that meets resistance everywhere usually means the entry point sits where the interests are densest. Enter where nobody objects and it moves itself.

### The parts · See the structure before you talk about technique
Ding's three stages — seeing a whole ox, ceasing to see a whole ox, meeting it with the spirit — are increasingly fine readings of structure. Technique is a by-product of that reading. Train it in the other order and you are training force.
e.g. A new hire handles a complaint with scripts. A veteran hears which step it's actually stuck at. The difference is the map in their head.

### The parts · Slow down where it knots
Ding isn't smooth throughout: at every knot he sees the difficulty, grows wary, slows, and makes his movements smaller. Real fluency isn't speed the whole way. It's knowing where you must go slowly.
e.g. For the two steps most likely to go wrong, add a check instead of adding speed. People with one tempo have all their accidents in one place.

### Q: How do I use it today?
Where you are: something is hard to push at every point, and you're considering pushing harder.
Ask first: is my blade in a gap or on a bone?
Where it goes wrong: substituting force for position; holding one tempo throughout and not slowing where you most need to.

### Lines to keep
The joints have space, the blade has no thickness.
At every knot I see the difficulty, grow wary, and slow down.
I meet it with the spirit and do not look with the eye.

========================================================================
## Zhuangzi · Things being equal
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/zhuangzi/equalizing-things/
Source: Zhuangzi, Discussion on Making All Things Equal
Tags: Deep read, Zhuangzi, Whose ruler is this

Two people argue to the end and neither is convinced. Why Zhuangzi says a third person won't settle it either.

### Q: What actually happened?
Zhuangzi asks an almost mischievous question. A person sleeping somewhere damp gets a bad back — does a loach? A person up a tree is frightened — is a monkey? Of the three, who knows the proper place to live? He extends the logic to argument: if you beat me in a debate, are you actually right? Bring a third person to judge, and whether they agree with you or with me they have already taken a side. How could they settle it? This isn't abolishing right and wrong. It's a reminder that right and wrong always speak from inside some standard.

### The parts · Before arguing, ask whose ruler is being used
There is a right and wrong on that side too, and one on this side. Most deadlocks aren't disputes about facts, they're disputes about standards — each conclusion holds inside its own. Until the standards are on the table, no amount of discussion converges.
e.g. Engineering says the design is good because it's maintainable; the business says it's bad because it ships late. Both are right. They're scoring different functions.

### The parts · The third party brings a standard too
Calling in a more senior person looks neutral and is really introducing a third standard. It ends the argument by authority rather than by understanding, so the same disagreement reappears unchanged the next time.
e.g. The boss rules and both teams comply. Three months later the identical fight happens on a different project.

### The parts · Move position and the ruler changes
Zhuangzi's method isn't finding the one correct ruler. It's acknowledging where your own came from. Do that and the other conclusion stops being 'wrong' and becomes 'true under his conditions' — and then you can discuss conditions instead of correctness.
e.g. Swap 'your plan won't work' for 'given we're prioritising the ship date, what does your plan cost?' Same subject, different conversation.

### Q: How do I use it today?
Where you are: a disagreement keeps recurring and never resolves.
Ask first: what is each side optimising? Can both targets hold at once?
Where it goes wrong: ending it by authority without touching the difference in standards; treating the other conclusion as an error rather than as correct under other conditions.

### Lines to keep
There is a right and wrong on that side, and one on this side.
If you beat me in the argument, are you actually right?
Of the three, who knows the proper place to live?

<!-- chapters:end -->
